This study investigates the identification of natural direct and indirect effects within a stratified case-control framework involving a binary exposure, a binary outcome, and a binary mediator. We demonstrate that these effects can be estimated using only four specific quantities derived from the strata-specific data. Furthermore, we establish that these quantities are estimable through four targeted maximum likelihood estimators (MLEs) designed for stratified case-control data. Our findings indicate that these MLEs achieve the optimal convergence rate of $n^{-1/2}$ and possess the optimal minimax rate of risk for squared error loss. Additionally, we present a simulation study to evaluate the performance of the proposed MLEs. Finally, we apply this methodology to analyze data from the Women's Health Initiative. The complete code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1999/MediationCaseControl. This work extends the methodology outlined in Chen and Robins (2014). The primary distinction lies in the binary nature of the mediator; in contrast, Chen and Robins (2014) address scenarios with continuous mediators, where natural direct and indirect effects are identified through seven distinct quantities. Consequently, the identification strategy and the construction of MLEs differ significantly between the two approaches. Specifically, the continuous mediator case requires the estimation of seven quantities, whereas the binary mediator case necessitates the estimation of only four. This reduction in the number of required quantities simplifies the identification and estimation processes. Additionally, the continuous mediator approach relies on the assumption of linearity, which is not required for the binary mediator method. Finally, the continuous mediator framework does not accommodate stratified case-control data, whereas our proposed method explicitly addresses this data structure. These distinctions highlight the unique contributions and applicability of our methodological extension. This study introduces a new method for learning from hindsight experiences, termed "hindsight summarization." The core concept involves resampling and relabeling past experiences to generate new training data. This process is driven by a contrastive value function that identifies the most informative states and actions relative to a specific outcome. We demonstrate that this approach is mathematically equivalent to contrastive policy gradient and contrastive value iteration. This study introduces a neural network-based framework for solving hyperbolic and parabolic partial differential equations (PDEs). The approach is grounded in the finite volume method, utilizing a cell-mean-based discretization of the spatial domain. A neural network is then employed to approximate the temporal evolution of the cell mean values. The network's parameters are optimized by minimizing the residual of the PDE at the cell centers and enforcing initial and boundary conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves high accuracy and exhibits robustness. Furthermore, the method is straightforward to implement and can be readily extended to address systems of PDEs. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmadrezaei/CNN-PDE. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the finite volume method; Section 3 details the CNN-PDE approach; Section 4 presents numerical results; and Section 5 offers concluding remarks. Additionally, Section 6 provides a comparison with the Fourier spectral method. The authors acknowledge the valuable comments and suggestions received from the reviewers. This paper examines the positivity of characteristic forms for globally defined vector bundles. We establish the positivity of the total Chern form and the total Todd form for any such bundle. Furthermore, we derive an equation linking the total characteristic form of a vector bundle to that of its direct summands via the push-forward map. As an application, we demonstrate that the positivity of the total Chern form is equivalent to that of the total Todd form. The paper concludes with a discussion of the theory's limitations and potential avenues for future research. This paper presents the design, development, and enhancement of high-power laser systems, alongside a demonstration of a reverse engineering technique. The primary objective is to create a high-power, high-energy laser system utilizing a high-Q factor, high-capacity, and high-efficiency master oscillator power amplifier (MOPA) architecture. Table-assisted question answering (TableQA) has garnered significant interest recently, with recent studies demonstrating that decomposing complex questions into simpler sub-questions can enhance performance. However, existing research primarily addresses unstructured questions, leaving the efficacy of decomposition for structured inputs like tables underexplored. This paper investigates the utility of decomposition specifically for table-oriented fact confirmation. We introduce a dataset comprising fact confirmation queries that require table decomposition, alongside a method to automatically generate such decomposition instructions. Our findings indicate that incorporating decomposition instructions yields only marginal improvements in F1 scores. Furthermore, we observe that the current state-of-the-art model, TabFact, already implicitly handles decomposition, rendering explicit instructions largely redundant. Consequently, we conclude that decomposition is not a critical factor for table-oriented fact confirmation and propose that future efforts should prioritize other strategies, such as enhancing the modeling of implicit questions within tables. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are powerful tools for creating realistic images, yet they struggle to generate samples conditioned on unstructured data like natural language due to the vast disparity between textual and visual feature spaces. To address this, we introduce a method that embeds unstructured inputs into a latent space compatible with the image generation process. By training a discriminator to distinguish between the GAN's generated images and those produced by combining the GAN with an autoencoder, we identify a shared latent space. This approach enables the generation of realistic images that align with the provided unstructured input. We validate this technique across various GAN architectures and datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in producing semantically relevant images. Furthermore, we show that the method can be utilized to train a classifier capable of assessing the relevance of generated images to specific inputs. Our results indicate that the approach performs robustly across different data distributions and GAN types, successfully generating images relevant to the input text. This paper investigates the contrast between two Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithms designed for Bayesian variable selection. The first algorithm, known as the reversible jump step sampler, was introduced by Green (1995) and is frequently employed in practice. The second is a recently developed method by Chen and Shao (2010) that utilizes a contrastive uniform sampling approach. We demonstrate that the contrast between these two algorithms is primarily driven by their distinct proposals for selecting the next model. Furthermore, we illustrate that the contrast between the algorithms can be significant in practical applications. Finally, we propose a new step sampler that integrates the advantages of both existing methods. This proposed algorithm exhibits superior performance compared to the other two algorithms in terms of mixing properties. The paper concludes with a numerical study to validate these claims. All proofs are provided in the appendix.

Keywords: Bayesian variable selection; contrastive uniform sampling; Markov chain Monte Carlo; reversible jump step sampler; variable screening.

Distance labeling for graphs assigns short labels to vertices such that the pairwise distance between any two vertices can be determined solely from their labels. While this concept was introduced over two decades ago, the most efficient labels for general graphs remain quadratic in size. This paper presents the first non-trivial distance labeling for planar graphs that is subquadratic, specifically achieving a size of $O(n^{7/6}\log n)$. Furthermore, our approach is robust against label corruption; even if a constant fraction of the labels are altered, the distance between any pair of vertices can still be accurately recovered. We also provide a nearly tight bound for triangulated planar graphs, demonstrating that any fault-resilient distance labeling for these graphs must be at least $\Omega(n^{5/6})$. Additionally, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(n^{3/4})$ for distance labelings in general graphs that tolerate a constant fraction of label faults. Finally, we extend our results to distance labeling schemes, proving that our upper and lower bounds for planar graphs hold true even when labels are permitted to depend on a parameter $k$. In this setting, the upper bound becomes $O(n^{7/6}\log n \cdot k)$ and the lower bound $\Omega(n^{5/6} \cdot k)$. Our findings also apply to graphs with bounded genus. Notably, our lower bound for triangulated planar graphs matches the upper bound for distance labeling schemes, indicating that our scheme is optimal for this graph class. Additionally, we present a distance labeling scheme for planar graphs with bounded degree that achieves a size of $O(n^{5/6}\log n \cdot k)$, which is nearly optimal given our lower bound for triangulated planar graphs. While recent research has explored various methods to identify anomalous data, this paper introduces a novel approach utilizing distributional normal processes (DNPs) to model the relationship between input features and network outputs. By representing outputs as random variables, DNPs can quantify the uncertainty of predictions for specific inputs. We propose leveraging this uncertainty to identify OOD data. Furthermore, we develop a multi-scale DNP layer that integrates multiple DNPs to enhance detection performance. This study examines a driven, open optical-lattice system featuring a scar-like state, where an external pump injects bosons into a flat band while a loss mechanism removes them from the highest energy levels. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, this setup triggers a nonequilibrium phase transition into a Bose-condensed state. This condensation is driven by heating within the Floquet framework, which causes the system to exit the stable region of its dynamical map. Furthermore, we show that this nonequilibrium Bose condensation can be interpreted as a novel form of Bose-Einstein condensation occurring in an effective non-Hermitian system. Finally, we explore the potential for observing this phenomenon experimentally. These findings highlight the significance of incorporating dissipation in the design of novel nonequilibrium quantum phases and offer a new method for investigating non-Hermitian physics. Additionally, this work establishes a new pathway for generating Bose-Einstein condensates in nonequilibrium settings. The research was conducted using the open-source Python package Qutip. This study introduces a statistical framework to characterize the timing behavior of non-repetitive optical clocks. The model's validity is confirmed through time-series analysis of experimental data from a single-photon-based optical clock, which demonstrates that the proposed approach effectively captures the clock's timing dynamics. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the time-series data adheres to a Gaussian distribution, a result that aligns with the central limit theorem. These insights are expected to advance the development of quantum networks and the realization of a quantum internet. Additionally, the research offers a novel perspective on the time-domain properties of optical clocks, a topic that has received limited attention in prior studies. Finally, the work underscores the critical role of quantum measurement in the operation of optical clocks. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the fundamental principles of optical clocks; Section 3 presents the experimental setup and methodology; Section 4 details the experimental results; Section 5 discusses the implications of these findings; and Section 6 provides the study's conclusions. This study introduces a real-time, cross-layer framework designed to restore services following network failures and mitigate faults within Software-Defined Networking (SDN) utilizing Service Function Chains (SFC). The proposed solution comprises two primary components: (1) an offline module responsible for SFC design and fault-tolerant failure restoration, and (2) an online module focused on fault mitigation and energy-efficient resource management. The offline component employs a two-stage approach: first, it generates an SFC design that minimizes total cost while satisfying constraints such as latency, bandwidth, and function availability; second, it establishes failure-restoration strategies that ensure restoration times remain below a specified threshold while minimizing the number of backup paths. The online component utilizes a real-time algorithm to dynamically adjust SFCs and network resources, thereby mitigating faults and optimizing energy consumption. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively reduces restoration durations and the count of backup paths, while simultaneously lowering total costs and energy usage. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness against network failures and faults, maintaining SFC performance even under high failure rates. Additionally, the approach demonstrates resilience against traffic fluctuations, ensuring SFC performance remains stable despite varying traffic loads. Finally, the proposed solution is adaptable to diverse network failure scenarios and fault types. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. Holographic error correction codes are defined by their classical error correction capabilities and the presence of power-law correlations. This study introduces a new class of codes, termed hyper-invariant MERA (hMERA), which maintains holographic properties while exhibiting power-law correlations. The hMERA code family is constructed by applying a renormalization group transformation to the Haar measure on the symmetric group $S_N$. As the system size $N$ increases, the code achieves a higher code rate and a minimum distance scaling as $N^{1/2}$. Furthermore, the correlation length of the Haar measure on $S_N$ scales with $N$ according to a power law, a property that is inherited by the hMERA code. Additionally, the code distance of hMERA is demonstrated to be proportional to the distance between the corresponding renormalization group transformations. These findings suggest that hMERA codes may serve as a valuable resource for quantum simulation. This study investigates the spatial distribution of filaments within the Galactic Core, specifically analyzing the distance between them. The analysis relies on a catalog of 1,000 filaments, where each entry includes a 3D position derived from the average distance to its constituent stars. The observed distribution of inter-filament distances aligns with a log-normal function, characterized by a mean distance of 0.15 pc and a standard deviation of 0.06 pc. This finding indicates that filaments are not uniformly distributed throughout the Galactic Core. Furthermore, the mean inter-filament distance is approximately 1.5 times larger than the mean intra-filament distance, suggesting that filaments are not isolated entities but rather form a continuous, thread-like structure. These results support the hypothesis that the Galactic Core is a turbulent medium, where filaments arise from the interaction between stellar winds and the surrounding interstellar medium. Additionally, the study examines the relationship between the number of stars in a filament and its length, finding that the data fits a power-law distribution with an index of 1.1. This distribution is consistent with the distribution of filament lengths across the entire Galactic Core. Finally, the analysis explores the correlation between filament length and the number of stars, revealing a strong correlation that reinforces the conclusion that filaments constitute a continuous structure within the Galactic Core. These findings are crucial for understanding the formation and evolution of the Galactic Core. The research was conducted using the Gaia Data Release 3. This study addresses optimal voltage reduction in integrated primary-secondary distribution networks featuring distributed energy resources (DERs). To achieve this, we introduce a distributed optimization framework that utilizes a distributed subgradient method for optimal voltage reduction. The approach incorporates a novel two-stage model designed to minimize power losses and DER costs while adhering to distribution system operational limits. The first stage involves formulating a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) problem to determine the optimal placement of DERs, whereas the second stage employs a convex optimization model to calculate the optimal tap positions for transformers and the reactive power output of DERs. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed distributed algorithm successfully solves the two-stage problem with high accuracy and rapid convergence. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits robustness against variations in network topology and network size. Finally, the proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing centralized and distributed approaches. The algorithm's effectiveness is validated through simulations on a 13-node test system and a real-world 12,600-node system in California. Additionally, the algorithm demonstrates strong scalability, maintaining efficiency even when applied to large-scale systems. This study examines a non-stochastic multi-armed bandit framework where arm-dependent delays occur with specific probabilities. We introduce a specialist algorithm designed to identify the optimal arm by maximizing the mean reward, even in the presence of these delays. Our analysis demonstrates that this approach achieves a regret bound of $O(T)$, where $T$ represents the total number of rounds. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(T)$ for any algorithm, indicating that no method can attain a regret bound superior to $O(T)$. Finally, we illustrate that the proposed specialist algorithm surpasses the delayed UCB algorithm in this specific setting. The paper concludes with a discussion of open questions. This paper introduces LEATHER, a new framework designed to generate text in conversational settings. The system employs a two-stage process: first, it conditions a text generation model on the conversation history to create a response, and second, it conditions a second model on that initial response to produce a revised version. This study introduces a statistical surrogate model for predicting loads on offshore wind turbines, utilizing chained Gaussian processes to capture the hierarchical dependencies among wind, turbine, and structural response data. The model's performance is evaluated against a dataset comprising 100,000 records of 10-minute time series for wind conditions, turbine states, and structural responses. This capability is illustrated through a case study involving an offshore wind turbine with a flexible tower. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. Social media platforms have become integral to our daily digital lives, offering a vast array of information. This study investigates Twitter data specifically regarding the Izmir earthquake. By analyzing the platform's structure and content, we examine the distribution of user followers and the frequency of hashtags. Furthermore, we explore the temporal evolution of hashtag usage to identify the most prevalent topics. The findings indicate that the data reveals a clear temporal pattern, with the most frequently used hashtags being #10Ekim, #izmir, #deprem, and #10ekim. Additionally, the data demonstrates that the majority of tweets originated from users with a limited number of followers. These results suggest that the event generated significant public interest, with the highest volume of activity occurring shortly after the earthquake. Ultimately, this research underscores the potential of Twitter data for analyzing social events. The source code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ozgurbayram/twitterdata. This paper demonstrates that the $R_\infty$ property is not preserved under nilpotent quotients when moving from non-nilpotent groups. Specifically, for any integer $n \geq 2$, the generalized Baumslag-Solitar group $G_n = \langle a, t \mid t a t^{-1} = a^n \rangle$ possesses this property; however, its nilpotent quotient $N_n = G_n / \gamma_{n+1}(G_n)$ does not. Furthermore, we establish that $N_n$ fails to have the $R_\infty$ property for all $n \geq 2$. Additionally, we prove that the metabelian quotient $N_2 = G_2 / \gamma_3(G_2)$ also does not exhibit the $R_\infty$ property. However, this approach is often hindered by the ill-posed nature of the problem, which typically results in unstable solutions. This work introduces a novel inversion technique that employs forward optimization within a trajectory framework. By minimizing the discrepancy between observed and simulated data while simultaneously regularizing the initial conditions, the method ensures stable reconstructions of the underlying system dynamics. These examples demonstrate that the method can accurately recover both the forward dynamics and initial conditions, even when dealing with sparse, noisy, and incomplete data. Furthermore, the approach is robust against data loss and capable of handling data with varying sampling rates. This paper introduces SceNDD, a situation-based naturalistic driving dataset designed to facilitate research on autonomous vehicle decision-making. Comprising 1,000 driving episodes, each lasting 10 to 20 seconds, the data was gathered using a mobile sensor suite. The dataset features 14 sensor modalities, including 10 high-frequency streams at 100 Hz (such as LiDAR, cameras, and IMU) and four low-frequency streams (such as GPS and OBD). We provide a detailed description of the data collection methodology and offer a comprehensive analysis of the recordings, covering data quality, sensor characteristics, and driving scenarios. Furthermore, we present a novel, open-source data processing pipeline that enables users to access the raw data and extract specific features. Finally, we demonstrate the dataset's utility by applying a reinforcement learning algorithm to solve a specific decision-making task. The entire dataset and processing pipeline are publicly available at https://github.com/SebastianKraemer/SceNDD. This resource is intended to support the development of data-driven decision-making models for autonomous vehicles. Additionally, we hope it will serve as a benchmark for evaluating new learning-based approaches in the field of autonomous driving. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 details the data collection process; Section 4 presents the data analysis; and Section 5 illustrates the application of the dataset to autonomous driving decision-making. The paper concludes with a discussion of the dataset's limitations and potential future directions. This theorem connects the probability distributions of forward and reverse paths, where "forward" and "reverse" refer to the system's evolution under distinct protocols. This paper demonstrates that this assumption can be relaxed. Specifically, we prove that the IFt remains valid for non-equilibrium initial states provided they satisfy the detailed balance condition. Furthermore, we show that the probabilities of forward and reverse paths can be determined non-invasively using two-time projection operators. Finally, we apply these findings to the quantum Otto cycle, deriving an efficiency bound for quantum heat engines. This bound is expressed in terms of the overlap between the initial and final states of the working substance. Additionally, we establish a link between this bound and the Jarzynski equality. Our results indicate that the IFt for single-energy assessments offers a valuable framework for analyzing the performance of quantum heat engines. We illustrate this by examining two specific cycles: the quantum Otto cycle and the quantum Carnot cycle. In both cases, we calculate the overlap between initial and final states and derive corresponding performance bounds. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the design of quantum heat engines. We demonstrate that the derived bound can be saturated by a specific protocol, which we term the "optimal protocol." This protocol enables the quantum Otto cycle to achieve the maximum possible efficiency allowed by the IFt. We conclude by discussing the broader implications of these findings for the development of quantum heat engines. Our analysis suggests that the IFt for single-energy assessments can serve as a fundamental tool for designing efficient quantum heat engines. By utilizing this theorem, researchers can establish performance bounds and identify optimal protocols for specific applications. This approach can facilitate the creation of more efficient and reliable quantum devices. We validate the effectiveness of this approach by presenting a proof-of-concept implementation based on the Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) framework. Our experimental results confirm that this mechanism successfully prevents social network reconstruction attacks. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed solution enables the app to notify users of potential close contacts, even in the absence of a COVID-19 diagnosis. These findings suggest that QANNs represent a promising avenue for developing quantum machine learning algorithms. This study investigates how Signal users perceive and understand the platform's two-factor authentication PINs. To explore the reasons behind this low comprehension, we conducted 15 in-depth interviews with users who hold incorrect beliefs about the PINs' function. Our analysis reveals that these misconceptions stem from users' lack of knowledge regarding the security and privacy features of messaging applications. Furthermore, we identified that users are more likely to misunderstand Signal's PINs when they are highly engaged with the app and possess a casual understanding of its features. These findings highlight the necessity for Signal to enhance user education on its security and privacy mechanisms. Additionally, we propose that developers should evaluate how their design decisions influence user comprehension and consider implementing strategies to improve it. Finally, we offer recommendations for researchers to better assess user understanding of their products. Solar irradiance, which varies with the sun's position, is a critical factor in modeling solar energy systems. This paper introduces a new numerical integration technique called Solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature (SWGQ), designed to efficiently and accurately compute integrals involving solar irradiance. The method is derived by applying a coordinate transformation to the classical Gaussian quadrature formula. Numerical experiments demonstrate that SWGQ achieves high accuracy with a minimal number of function evaluations, outperforming the trapezoidal rule and Simpson's rule. Furthermore, the study examines the method's convergence behavior and its application to solving ordinary differential equations. These findings indicate that SWGQ is particularly effective for integrating functions with solar irradiance weights, offering a valuable tool for researchers and engineers working in solar energy integration. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/SWGQ. Additionally, the paper includes a case study on the solar photovoltaic system of the International Space Station (ISS), with the corresponding code available at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/SWGQ_ISS. The generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix is a fundamental component in various machine learning applications, including meta-learning, multi-task learning, and neural network pruning. However, its computational demands are substantial, particularly when dealing with extensive datasets and high-dimensional parameter spaces. This study introduces ViViT, a novel matrix structure that offers an efficient approximation of the GGN, enabling rapid computation. ViViT is constructed by decomposing the GGN into a series of low-rank matrices, which facilitates the calculation of eigenvalues and eigenvectors. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the GGN can be expressed as the product of two matrices derived from the Hessian of the loss function with respect to the data. This insight allows for the development of a more precise low-rank approximation of the GGN. Additionally, we present a theoretical analysis of the error associated with this low-rank approximation. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of ViViT through experiments conducted on image classification and recommendation tasks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/SeongJinKim/ViViT. We establish that for any fixed dimension $d \geq 2$ and prime $p$, there exists a constant $C(d,p)$ such that an arithmetic lattice $\Gamma$ within a simple, non-compact, adjoint-type algebraic group $G$ defined over a number field $k$, which is $p$-adically split at all places outside a set $S$ of cardinality $|S|=d$, exhibits rigidity modulo $p$ with constant $C(d,p)$ provided $S$ is sufficiently large. This finding extends the work of Bourgain, Gamburd, and Sarnak (2016) from the case where $k=\mathbb{Q}$ and $d=2$ to arbitrary dimensions and number fields. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this result is optimal with respect to the dimension $d$. Our findings rely on a novel concept termed "charmability," which serves as a higher-dimensional analogue to the non-vanishing of the Mobius function on maximal parabolic subgroups. Additionally, we present an unconditional version of this result for algebraic groups of type $A_n$ over number fields, contingent upon the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. Finally, we explore applications of our findings to the study of Hecke operators acting on modular forms. Object pose estimation is a critical task in computer vision, yet it remains difficult due to the need for precise localization and orientation. While current state-of-the-art methods achieve high accuracy, they depend heavily on large datasets containing numerous annotated instances. This paper introduces a zero-shot, class-level pose estimation approach that requires no training data. By leveraging a pre-trained vision-language model to map class names to pose embeddings, our method enables pose estimation for any object class without prior examples. We evaluate this approach on the 80-class Panoptic Segmentation Dataset (PanopticSeg) and the 10-class Pascal Context Dataset (PContext), demonstrating superior performance in zero-shot, class-level pose estimation. Graph data is frequently incomplete, necessitating the ability to answer queries regarding missing information. This study introduces VACA, a method for learning interventional and counterfactual queries from partial observations of a graph. VACA employs a latent variable model to represent the graph's generative process, utilizing a variational graph autoencoder to approximate the intractable latent posterior. The model is trained via maximum likelihood, with the latent space designed to capture the graph's Markov structure. We demonstrate that VACA can accurately answer queries concerning missing data and validate its effectiveness through both synthetic and real-world experiments. The Irish LOFAR station, situated in Birr, Co. Offaly, Ireland, has been operating since 2014. In 2019, a new backend was introduced to the Irish station to facilitate the REAL-time Transient Collection (REALTA) project. This system is designed to identify and record radio transients in real time, enabling the rapid dissemination of alerts to the global transient community. This paper outlines the REALTA system's architecture and describes its initial performance regarding transient detection and localization. Additionally, we present a selection of radio transients recorded by REALTA, including Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs), Pulsars, and Galactic and Extragalactic Fast Transients. We also provide a comprehensive list of all FRBs detected by REALTA, which can be accessed via the project's website. Furthermore, we detail the development of a new data reduction pipeline that allows for the offline re-analysis of REALTA data. This pipeline is currently being utilized to re-process the data to enhance the sensitivity of the transient search. Finally, we discuss the potential for using REALTA data to investigate the relationship between FRBs and Fast Blue Optical Transients (FBOTs). This study examines the impact of pre-released film attributes on box office revenue. This study presents a novel method for analyzing blazar spectra, specifically targeting the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excesses observed in these sources. The methodology relies on a Monte-Carlo simulation of particle interactions within a blazar jet, incorporating a realistic treatment of jet geometry and magnetic field structures. The model posits that the UV/soft X-ray excess arises from inverse Compton scattering of synchrotron photons emitted by electrons in the jet, a process referred to as internal external-Compton scattering. This approach is applied to the spectra of two blazars, 3C 273 and Mrk 421, to demonstrate the technique's utility. The analysis reveals that the model can successfully reproduce the spectral energy distributions of both objects. Furthermore, the study establishes that the magnetic field strength in the jet is approximately 100 microGauss, and the electron population follows a power-law distribution with an index of roughly 2.5. These findings are consistent with the blazar jet model proposed by Ghisellini et al. (2004). Additionally, the results indicate that the jet is highly relativistic, with a Lorentz factor of approximately 10. Finally, the paper discusses the potential of this method for analyzing the spectra of other blazars. The source code used for the Monte-Carlo simulations is available at https://github.com/abdelrahmanmohamed1994/MAPPIES. This work is the second in a series; the first paper, MAPPIES I, is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.00001. The acronym MAPPIES stands for "Monte-Carlo Analysis of Partially Polarized Inverse External-Compton Scattering." The analytical extension of a function from a real domain to a complex one is a fundamental concept in complex analysis. This paper introduces a novel approach to analytically extending real-variable functions over complex domains, grounded in the observation that the fractional Laplacian of a function $f$ can be expressed as the second derivative of its Hilbert transform. This insight enables the definition of the fractional Laplacian for real-valued functions on complex domains, thereby facilitating the analytical extension of functions originally defined on real domains. The proposed method is validated through numerical experiments involving the sine function and the fractional Laplacian. Furthermore, the work explores the fractional gradient and Laplacian of functions defined on complex domains, offering a new perspective on complex-valued functions. Finally, the paper examines the analytical extension of the Gaussian function, revealing that the complex Gaussian is not the unique extension of the Gaussian function. These findings are anticipated to have significant applications in physics, particularly in the study of complex fluids. Additionally, the methodology is expected to be valuable for researchers in complex analysis and function theory. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. We introduce a digital identification framework for symmetric pure states, enabling the approximate cloning of an unknown state with a specified success probability. This approach is realized through a sequence of unitary transformations applied to multiple copies of the state, followed by a measurement on the output of the first transformed copy. The scheme achieves an optimal trade-off between the number of copies required and the probability of successful identification. Furthermore, we derive an exact expression for the optimal success probability and establish a novel upper bound for it. These findings are applicable to states within any finite-dimensional Hilbert space. Additionally, we extend the analysis to scenarios involving infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces, specifically focusing on coherent states. In these cases, we determine the optimal success probability and provide an upper bound for it. Finally, we examine the problem of identifying a single unknown state from a set of non-orthogonal states. For this scenario, we calculate the optimal success probability for both finite and infinite-dimensional spaces. In the finite-dimensional case, we also present a method to construct the optimal measurement. For infinite-dimensional spaces, we derive an upper bound for the optimal success probability. Baryon production is investigated through the quantized fragmentation of a QCD filament, which is modeled as a helical, charged, color-charged, and quantized string. This filament is assumed to originate from the initial state of a heavy-ion collision. The analysis demonstrates that baryon production can be interpreted as the fragmentation of this filament into a sequence of baryons. Furthermore, the model successfully reproduces the experimentally observed rapidity distributions of both baryons and antibaryons. Additionally, the filament's charge and color charges are shown to generate the necessary sea quarks and gluons. The study also examines the filament's response to external fields, such as those present in heavy-ion collisions, and its interaction with the quark-gluon plasma. Finally, the filament is proposed as a viable candidate for the QCD string within the Lund model. The paper concludes with a discussion of the model's predictions and potential applications. North-south travel-time measurements in helioseismology are influenced by both global and local phenomena. While global effects, such as solar rotation, are well understood, local effects arising from active regions remain poorly characterized. This study examines how active regions impact these measurements by analyzing the contributions of oscillation modes with different spherical degrees ($l$) and azimuthal orders ($m$). The analysis utilizes a dataset of 1,000 active regions observed by the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager (HMI) on the Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO). Results indicate that for $l \leq 100$, the primary local effect is a shift in the mean travel time caused by the active region, with a magnitude of approximately 100 nanoseconds. This shift scales with the region's area and is more pronounced in modes with lower $l$ and $m$. Conversely, the local effect on the travel-time gradient is significantly smaller, estimated at around 10 nanoseconds. Furthermore, the impact of active regions on the travel-time gradient diminishes as the spherical degree $l$ increases. These findings suggest that the local effects of active regions on the travel-time gradient are negligible for $l \leq 100$. Additionally, the study demonstrates that active regions can be identified by examining the travel-time gradient as a function of $l$ and $m$. Finally, the paper explores the potential for using these measurements to quantify the local effects of active regions. These insights are crucial for interpreting the global effects of solar rotation and solar-like oscillations on travel-time measurements. Ultimately, this research aids in understanding the Sun's internal rotation and the behavior of solar-like oscillations. Small-area estimation (SAE) is a statistical approach used to derive reliable estimates for small geographic regions, such as districts or neighborhoods. This paper reviews the design-based and model-based methodologies employed in SAE, with a specific focus on their application in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). It examines the advantages and constraints of each approach within this context and compares their performance through a simulation study. The findings indicate that model-based methods generally yield more precise estimates than design-based methods, although model-based techniques are currently underutilized in LMICs. The study concludes by offering recommendations for future research and practical implementation. Specifically, it advocates for the adoption of model-based SAE methods in LMICs, the integration of these methods into national statistical surveys, and the development of user-friendly software to facilitate their implementation. Additionally, the paper recommends that software developers prioritize the inclusion of model-based SAE capabilities in their tools. Finally, the authors suggest that researchers and practitioners in LMICs collaborate to address the challenges associated with implementing model-based SAE, thereby enhancing the quality of small-area estimates in these regions. The paper also provides a detailed example of model-based SAE implementation using R software. This example demonstrates how to estimate poverty rates in small areas using data from the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) and the Multiple Indicator Cluster Surveys (MICS). The authors hope this example will serve as a practical guide for researchers and practitioners interested in implementing model-based SAE in LMICs. The R code used to generate the example is available on GitHub. The Kelly criterion serves as a foundational principle in risk management and investment, determining the optimal fraction of a bankroll to wager in order to maximize long-term wealth growth. This study extends the classical Kelly framework by incorporating quantum mechanics, specifically treating the reward as a quantum state. We demonstrate that the optimal betting fraction remains constant when the reward is defined as a mixture of winning and losing probabilities. Furthermore, we establish that the optimal fraction is non-zero only when the winning probability distribution exhibits non-classicality, quantified by its relative entropy of entanglement. Additionally, we prove that the optimal betting fraction is non-zero exclusively when the winning probability distribution is entangled. These findings indicate that the proposed betting strategy can generate profits even when the winning probability is non-local, provided the source of these probabilities is entangled. Finally, we examine the impact of decoherence on the betting fraction and observe that it diminishes as decoherence increases. This work offers a novel perspective on applying the Kelly criterion to quantum systems and may have significant implications for quantum finance. Our results suggest that the quantum Kelly criterion could be valuable for managing risk in quantum systems, such as quantum computers, and for developing new strategies in quantum finance. We present a three-dimensional hydrodynamical simulation of the collapse of a pre-stellar core to form a protostar, incorporating a simplified model of magnetic braking. Our results indicate that the core's magnetic field is efficiently transported to the circumstellar disk, where it is amplified by the disk's differential rotation. This process generates a magnetically active disk with a surface magnetic field reaching approximately 100 G at 100 au. The simulation also reveals a prominent gap at 10 au, caused by the magnetospheric truncation of the disk. Furthermore, we observe that the disk's surface temperature is significantly elevated due to the absorption of X-rays produced by the central star. These findings align with recent observations of the T Tauri star TW Hya, which exhibits a disk surface temperature of roughly 1000 K at 10 au and a magnetic field strength of about 100 G at 100 au. Consequently, our model successfully reproduces the physical characteristics of TW Hya, suggesting that the star's properties can be explained by the collapse of a pre-stellar core. Additionally, we demonstrate that the magnetic field within the disk can be detected via the Zeeman effect in the 21 cm line of neutral hydrogen. Finally, we show that the magnetic field can be mapped using the circular polarization of the 21 cm line, offering a potential method for observing the magnetic field structure of protostars. These results underscore the critical role of magnetic fields in the formation of protostars and their disks. Our findings also suggest that the magnetic field structure of TW Hya can be investigated using the SKA and its precursors. Atmospheric variation is a critical factor in the precision of exoplanet transmission spectroscopy. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of atmospheric variability across a wide range of parameters, including planet radius, equilibrium temperature, and the abundances of H$_2$O, CO$_2$, and CH$_4$. We utilize the publicly available \texttt{petitRADTRANS} radiative transfer code to generate transmission spectra for 1,000,000 synthetic planets, incorporating both time-averaged and time-resolved observations. Our results indicate that the amplitude of atmospheric variation scales linearly with the abundances of H$_2$O, CO$_2$, and CH$_4$, as well as with the planet radius. Conversely, the variation amplitude decreases as the planet's equilibrium temperature rises. Furthermore, we observe that time-resolved observations yield significantly higher variation amplitudes compared to time-averaged data. These findings are essential for accurately interpreting future exoplanet observations. We also provide a Python package, \texttt{atmospheric\_variation}, to facilitate the application of these results. This tool enables users to calculate the expected variation amplitude for a given planet and to determine the necessary signal-to-noise ratio for a specific observation. Such capabilities are vital for designing future observing campaigns and assessing the feasibility of detecting atmospheric variations. We introduce a dual-field quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol that eliminates the need for phase stabilization. In this approach, Alice transmits two optical fields with orthogonal polarizations to Bob, where the phase difference between them is encoded with the field's polarization state. Bob performs joint measurements on these fields to decode the information. This method offers two primary benefits: first, it removes the requirement for phase stabilization, thereby simplifying the system; second, it achieves a higher key generation rate compared to existing single-field QKD schemes. We have analyzed the security of this dual-field protocol and demonstrated that it remains secure against general attacks. Furthermore, we have evaluated its performance under realistic conditions. Our results indicate that the dual-field protocol can generate keys at a rate of 1.2 Mbps over a distance of 100 meters using a 100 MHz bandwidth, with a signal-to-noise ratio of 1.0 dB. Additionally, we show that the protocol can extend the maximum transmission distance to 150 meters when the bandwidth is reduced to 10 MHz. These findings suggest that the dual-field QKD scheme is highly promising for practical applications. Finally, we have compared our dual-field protocol with the single-field QKD scheme proposed by Wang et al. [Phys. Rev. A 104, 022603 (2021)]. Our analysis reveals that the dual-field protocol outperforms the single-field version in both key generation rate and transmission distance. Consequently, the dual-field QKD scheme represents a significant advancement in the field of quantum communication. We evaluate our method on the VisDrone and PASCAL-Part datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting objects with open lexicons. We present a new study on the gas distribution surrounding the Rho Oph S1 star, utilizing a multi-wavelength analysis of ionized gas, atomic hydrogen, and molecular clouds. By combining data from the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and the Very Large Array (VLA), we mapped the ionized gas structure, while the IRAM 30m telescope provided observations of the PDR and atomic hydrogen. Our findings reveal a complex, asymmetric ionized gas distribution that extends up to 0.1 pc from the star, with a peak ionization fraction of 10% at 0.01 pc. The PDR exhibits a distinct morphology characterized by a bright, narrow ridge aligned with the atomic hydrogen shell, which is situated 0.01 pc from the star. This PDR is embedded within the atomic shell and extends into the molecular cloud, where it appears as a bright ridge. The atomic hydrogen shell displays a shell-like structure with a radius of 0.01 pc and a thickness of 0.005 pc, while the molecular cloud shows a shell-like morphology with a radius of 0.02 pc and a thickness of 0.01 pc. We propose that the ionized gas and PDR are driven by the stellar wind, whereas the atomic and molecular shells are shaped by the interaction between the stellar wind and the ambient interstellar medium. Furthermore, the PDR and atomic hydrogen shells are likely influenced by the ambient magnetic field. Finally, we suggest that the molecular cloud shell may have been formed by the interaction between the ambient interstellar medium and the Rho Oph S1 star. These results offer valuable insights into the interaction between massive stars and their surrounding interstellar medium. Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has demonstrated significant potential for automatically discovering high-performing neural network architectures. However, a persistent challenge in NAS is the interference problem, where the performance of an architecture is compromised when evaluated within a specific search space. This issue stems from the fact that the search space is merely a subset of the entire architecture space, causing performance to fluctuate across different spaces. Consequently, architectures that excel in one search space may fail to generalize to others, hindering the discovery of robust solutions. To address this, we introduce a novel method to mitigate interference by training multiple models in parallel and selecting the architecture with the highest average performance. Experimental results on the Cifar10 and Cifar100 datasets confirm the effectiveness of this approach, showing that it consistently identifies architectures with superior generalization capabilities. We demonstrate that any geodesically complete CAT(0) area possesses non-positive curvature at its boundary. Furthermore, we establish that for any compact, geodesically complete CAT(0) area, the boundary is either a simple closed curve or exhibits a cut locus of measure zero. Additionally, we prove that the boundary of a compact, geodesically complete CAT(0) surface is locally connected. Finally, we present a characterization of when the boundary of a compact, geodesically complete CAT(0) area is locally connected: this occurs if and only if the area is not homeomorphic to the closed unit disk. This result extends a theorem by P. Scott regarding closed surfaces. The proofs rely on a novel isoperimetric inequality applicable to geodesically complete CAT(0) areas. As an application, we confirm that the boundaries of compact, geodesically complete CAT(0) surfaces are uniformly locally connected. This finding strengthens a result by P. Scott concerning closed surfaces and offers an alternative proof of his theorem regarding the non-positive curvature of the boundaries of compact, geodesically complete CAT(0) surfaces. The article concludes with several open questions. The primary tools employed are the isoperimetric inequality, the structure of cut loci, and the theory of rectifiable sets. We anticipate that these methods will be valuable in addressing other boundary-related issues within the CAT(0) context. We establish sum rules for energy absorption within open scattering systems, specifically for a scalar field in anti-de Sitter space coupled to an external source. These rules constrain the absorption eigenvalues across all frequencies and remain valid even when the system exhibits chaos. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these sum rules are satisfied in holographic models representing both deconfined and confining strongly-coupled plasmas. Our findings indicate that the relaxation dynamics of energy absorption in these plasmas are governed by a small set of eigenvalues, a characteristic that may extend to more general systems. Additionally, we derive a sum rule for energy absorption in systems displaying level repulsion, a property that is also fulfilled by holographic plasmas. Finally, we discuss the connection between our results and the spectral form factor. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are widely recognized for their ability to extract spatially localized features, a capability attributed to the convolutional operation. However, recent studies indicate that fully connected networks (FCNs) can also achieve high performance on image classification tasks. This paper investigates whether FCNs can learn spatially localized features without relying on convolutional operations. We demonstrate that this is feasible by employing trimming, a regularization technique that eliminates redundant weights. Our findings reveal that the weights within trimmed FCNs are sparse and localized, mirroring the characteristics of CNNs. The valley degree of freedom in two-dimensional materials is a promising candidate for next-generation valleytronic devices. However, the valley index is not perfectly conserved due to various scattering mechanisms, including electron-phonon interactions, which can significantly alter valley physics. This study employs a first-principles approach to investigate how different electron-phonon interaction mechanisms affect valley physics in two-dimensional materials. Our findings indicate that the influence of these mechanisms varies across different two-dimensional systems. Specifically, in graphene, interactions with out-of-plane phonons are the primary factor in valley relaxation, whereas in silicene, in-plane phonons play the dominant role. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the impact of electron-phonon interactions on valley physics can be effectively modeled using a simplified valley relaxation rate equation. This work provides a comprehensive understanding of electron-phonon interaction effects on valley physics in two-dimensional materials, offering valuable insights for the design of valleytronic devices. Additionally, the methodology used to calculate electron-phonon interactions and valley relaxation rates is applicable to other two-dimensional materials. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective method for visual domain adaptation, achieving the highest scores in the NeurIPS 2022 Visual Domain Adaptation Challenge. The approach utilizes a teacher-student framework where the teacher is a pre-trained ResNet50 model, and the student is a lightweight network comprising a single convolutional layer followed by a fully connected layer. The study evaluates the method's performance across three tasks: image classification, semantic segmentation, and keypoint detection. The source domain is ImageNet, while the target domains consist of the CUB-200, PASCAL VOC, and COCO datasets for the respective tasks. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that a teacher-student framework can be successfully applied to all three tasks. Finally, the paper explores the impact of various hyperparameters on the method's performance. The results suggest that the proposed approach is simple, effective, and capable of delivering competitive performance across diverse tasks. The authors hope this work will inspire future research in visual domain adaptation. t-SNE is a widely used method for visualizing high-dimensional data by mapping it to a 2D plane. However, it fails to preserve local structures effectively and is unsuitable for spherical data. To address these limitations, we introduce VMF-SNE, a novel algorithm designed for visualizing spherical data. This approach integrates the von Mises-Fisher distribution with t-SNE, enabling the learning of a low-dimensional representation that maintains local structures while accommodating spherical data characteristics. Experimental results demonstrate that VMF-SNE outperforms t-SNE in both visual quality and quantitative metrics. Furthermore, we show that VMF-SNE surpasses other existing spherical data representation techniques, such as Stiefel-SNE and von Mises SNE. We examine the two-dimensional Fermi polaron, consisting of a mobile impurity interacting with a Fermi sea of mobile particles via an attractive potential. By employing a diagrammatic Monte Carlo approach, we calculate the ground-state energy as a function of the interaction strengths for both the polaron and the background Fermi sea. Our findings reveal a distinct polaronic regime where the impurity is tightly bound to a few background particles, alongside a broader regime where the polaron is weakly bound. We also analyze the system's behavior in the non-interacting limit. Furthermore, we compare our results with those from the large-N approximation and the variational method. Finally, we explore the implications of our findings for the superfluid phase transition. These results are supported by supplementary material, including a video of the polaron's dynamics. This method utilizes a fermionic quantum simulator featuring native two-body interactions between identical particles, alongside digital single-qubit gates. Furthermore, we establish that the method's accuracy is constrained by the hybrid's computational power, which is defined as the minimum of the digital and analog components. We establish general theorems regarding the nontrivial zeros of specific series of polynomials that arise from the spectral properties of graphs, with the aim of determining the stability of graph traits under minor perturbations. These findings are applied to two distinct families of polynomials. The first family is linked to the spectrum of a graph $G$ through the eigenvalues of its line graph $L(G)$, and we derive stability results for graph parameters associated with $G$ by utilizing the location of the zeros of these polynomials. The second family involves polynomials derived from the eigenvalues of the adjacency matrix for graphs with a fixed number of vertices, specifically those with a large spectral radius. We demonstrate that the zeros of these polynomials converge to a limiting function, which is analytic within a specific domain. This domain is notably larger than the unit disk, thereby yielding stability results for graph parameters defined on graphs with a fixed vertex count. Additionally, we present numerical computations of the zeros for these polynomials. Finally, we offer a unified perspective on these results by employing the framework of random regular graphs. In this context, graph parameters are represented as functions of the graph's spectrum, and we prove that, with high probability, these functions remain stable under small perturbations of the spectrum. This approach provides a natural explanation for the stability of graph parameters in both families. Furthermore, we extend these findings to the setting of quantum graphs. Our work relies on a novel method for analyzing the zeros of polynomial sequences, which we believe will find applications in other areas of graph theory. We anticipate that this methodology will also be valuable for investigating the stability of graph parameters in the broader context of random graphs. This study investigates how telecommuting impacts Scrum project success. Through a survey of 100 Scrum teams, we identified that success is significantly influenced by the frequency of telecommuting, the number of remote participants, and the proportion of remote workers. Furthermore, we examined how the distribution of remote versus on-site team members affects these success metrics. To validate our survey findings, we conducted a case study involving 1200 lines of code from two projects: one with a fully remote team and another with a mixed on-site and remote team. Our analysis revealed that the remote team exhibited superior code quality, lower defect rates, and higher test coverage compared to the hybrid team. These results corroborate the survey data, demonstrating that Scrum projects achieve greater success when executed entirely remotely rather than with a combination of remote and on-site personnel. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for organizations adopting Scrum and transitioning to remote work. The paper concludes by outlining potential directions for future research. This study examines a $K$-user interference network where each node possesses $N$ antennas and transmits to its intended destination while facing interference from other nodes. We analyze the General Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) for two scenarios: one allowing optimal power regulation and another restricting it to binary levels. Our findings indicate that the maximum GDoF advantage gained from optimal power control, compared to binary regulation, scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ antennas per node. This result contrasts with the $K$-user X-channel, where the benefit of optimal power control is limited to $\Theta(1)$, and with the $K$-user Y-channel, where no such benefit exists. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ advantage is achieved when the number of antennas per node is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. In this specific regime, we establish that the GDoF benefit of optimal power control over binary regulation is precisely $\sqrt{K}$. This conclusion is derived from a general interference alignment scheme utilizing optimal power regulation, which achieves a GDoF of $\sqrt{K}$, and a binary power control scheme achieving a GDoF of $\sqrt{K}-1$, both applicable to any $N$-antenna user interference network. Additionally, we prove that for any $N$-antenna user interference network, the GDoF benefit of optimal power control relative to binary power control does not exceed $\sqrt{K}$. Finally, we extend these results to the $K$-user X-channel and Y-channel, confirming that the corresponding GDoF benefits remain $\Theta(1)$ and $0$, respectively. These findings are also applicable to the $K$-user X-channel and Y-channel with side information. The paper concludes with a discussion on the implications of these results. This study addresses the creation of timetables for multiple tasks, where each task comprises a sequence of operations that may be processed concurrently. The objective is to minimize the total duration of the resulting schedule. We demonstrate that this multitasking timetabling problem is NP-hard and provide a polynomial-time algorithm for the case of two tasks with uniform processing times. Furthermore, we present a pseudo-polynomial algorithm applicable when task lengths are restricted to two distinct values. Finally, we evaluate the performance of these proposed algorithms through computational experiments. The results indicate that the algorithm's performance degrades as the number of tasks increases, though it remains effective for instances with a small number of tasks. Additionally, the algorithm exhibits superior performance when task lengths are uniform. However, when task lengths vary significantly, the algorithm's performance deteriorates. Consequently, we introduce a heuristic approach that demonstrates better performance under such conditions. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. Firmware upgrades are essential for maintaining the security and functionality of Internet of Things (IoT) devices. However, the heterogeneous nature of IoT architectures and the necessity for large-scale deployments in real-world settings often result in unreliable update mechanisms. Our evaluation demonstrates that this new protocol effectively mitigates the problems found in the original implementation. We hope this study will inspire further advancements in dependable firmware update mechanisms for IoT devices. We investigate the multifractal characteristics of the Fock-space propagator within the one-dimensional spin-1/2 XXZ model, which undergoes a transition from a delocalized to a localized phase as the interaction strength increases. Our analysis reveals that the scaling exponents of these multifractal properties remain constant across the entire range of interaction values, even extending beyond the critical point into the localized regime. This finding indicates that the shift in the critical interaction value, known as the many-body shift, does not alter the fundamental nature of the multifractal spectrum. Instead, the observed shift in the critical point is attributed to the presence of a finite-size gap in the excitation spectrum. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the asymptotic behavior of the spin-spin correlation function in the localized phase is governed by the same set of universal scaling exponents. These results suggest that the spin-spin correlation function in the localized phase retains a power-law form, thereby challenging the conventional view that localized states must decay exponentially. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings for the study of many-body localization. This paper addresses the challenge of identifying $k$ targets within a search space using a budget-limited interactive search algorithm. The algorithm operates by querying the user, who responds with a single bit of information. We introduce a new metric, $k$-robustness, to evaluate the performance of these algorithms. We demonstrate that the maximum achievable $k$-robustness equals the minimum size of a $k$-cover for the search space. Furthermore, we provide a polynomial-time algorithm to compute this value when $k$ is fixed. Additionally, we establish that determining the maximum $k$-robustness is NP-hard for any $k \geq 2$. Finally, we present a polynomial-time algorithm that calculates a $k$-robustness value within a factor of $O(k)$ of the optimal. Our approach is based on a reduction from the $k$-clique problem. We also explore the relationship between $k$-robustness and the $k$-cover problem. Finally, we extend our findings to the scenario where the search space evolves over time. In this dynamic setting, we prove that the problem remains NP-hard and that our proposed algorithm maintains an approximation ratio of $O(k)$. We also examine the connection between this dynamic problem and the $k$-set cover problem. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. Deep neural networks (DNNs) are highly susceptible to adversarial attacks, which can cause them to misclassify inputs with high confidence. While prior research has focused on creating adversarial examples to test and enhance DNN robustness, this study investigates the inherent robustness of quantum classifiers. We demonstrate that quantum classifiers possess a natural resilience against adversarial examples, rendering them largely immune to such attacks. Consequently, we propose a novel attack strategy targeting the global adversarial instances and disturbances of quantum classifiers. This approach successfully generates adversarial examples that deceive quantum classifiers, thereby revealing their vulnerabilities. Furthermore, we examine the robustness of quantum classifiers against adversarial disturbances, showing that these attacks can significantly degrade classifier performance. Our experimental results indicate that the proposed attack methods are effective against quantum classifiers, including those trained with adversarial examples. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for the future development of quantum machine learning. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/QuantumMLResearch/QMLOpenSource. Temporal planning is a well-established challenge within artificial intelligence, characterized by its capacity to model intricate problems and its proven tractability. However, the absence of a unified formalism for defining temporal planning problems has hindered the development of formally verified planning algorithms. This paper introduces a formalism for temporal planning and provides an official semantics based on linear temporal logic. Furthermore, we present formally verified algorithms for validating temporal planning problems and determining satisfiability. Our approach relies on a novel encoding of temporal planning into satisfiability modulo theories (SMT), which we demonstrate is both sound and complete. This paper establishes the global-in-time well-posedness of the Vlasov-Poisson system within a bounded, convex domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ featuring a $C^2$ boundary. The system incorporates specular reflection at the boundary and includes a source term $S(t,x,v)$ that is polynomially bounded in velocity and periodic in time. The proof relies on the regularity of weak solutions, which are derived through an $L^p$-estimate for the electric field. This estimate is achieved by demonstrating the uniform boundedness of the electric field in $L^p(\mathbb{R}^3)$ for all $p \in [1,+\infty)$, a result grounded in the regularity of the initial data. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the electric field possesses time derivatives of any order, thereby confirming the global existence of weak solutions. These findings extend previous results by providing a rigorous proof of well-posedness for the Vlasov-Poisson system in a confined region of $\mathbb{R}^3$. Additionally, the methodology is applicable to other kinetic models, such as the Vlasov-Maxwell system in confined domains. The analysis also addresses the regularity of the electric field near the boundary, a critical issue for future investigations into the long-time behavior of Vlasov-Poisson systems in confined spaces. Finally, the paper examines the impact of the source term $S(t,x,v)$ on the system's well-posedness. While the primary focus is on a polynomially bounded source term, the approach can be adapted to handle more complex scenarios, including non-polynomially bounded sources, provided the source function exhibits sufficient regularity. This flexibility allows for the consideration of various applications, such as modeling particle injection or absorption at the boundary. The study concludes by outlining several open questions and potential avenues for future research. These include the investigation of the long-time behavior of solutions, the development of numerical methods for solving the system, and the exploration of related problems in confined domains. The authors emphasize the significance of their findings for advancing the understanding of the Vlasov-Poisson system in confined regions and its applications across physics and engineering. Ultimately, this work represents a significant contribution to the field of kinetic theory and its applications. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the problem formulation and main results; Section 3 provides the proof of the main theorem; and Section 4 discusses open problems and future research directions

Concept positioning involves identifying the location of a specific concept within a text document. This paper introduces STRICT, a data retrieval-based approach that leverages search term recognition to determine concept positions. We demonstrate that STRICT surpasses state-of-the-art methods on the ConceptNet55 position dataset. Additionally, we present a case study on the ConceptNet55 attribute dataset to evaluate STRICT's performance in attribute position prediction. The code and data required to replicate our experiments are accessible at https://github.com/ruixuanwang/strict. Our findings indicate that STRICT can effectively predict concept positions in both general and specific domains. The results also reveal that STRICT is more robust against noisy data compared to other data retrieval-based search term recognition methods. Furthermore, we show that STRICT can be readily adapted to other position prediction tasks by simply replacing the knowledge base. Finally, we highlight that STRICT is computationally efficient, capable of predicting concept positions in a single forward pass. The source code is available at https://github.com/ruixuanwang/strict.

This study introduces a novel rheo-acoustic setup designed to probe the mechanical properties of colloidal gels while simultaneously modifying their structure through ultrasonic vibrations. The system's acoustic component delivers focused, continuous ultrasonic energy to the sample, allowing for real-time rheological measurements. We demonstrate that applying ultrasonic vibrations to a colloidal gel results in a reversible reduction in its storage modulus. Furthermore, by controlling the ultrasonic power, we can continuously tune the gel's mechanical properties and its response to shear. Finally, we show that these rheo-acoustic adjustments can be utilized to regulate the yield stress of the gel. These findings establish a foundation for future research into the structure and dynamics of colloidal gels under ultrasonic fields. Additionally, the proposed methodology is applicable to a wide range of colloidal systems, including those exhibiting shear thickening, shear banding, and jamming transitions. Ultimately, this work opens new avenues for manipulating the rheological properties of colloidal materials. Stable Matching is a widely used mechanism for allocating resources, such as school seats or jobs, based on the preferences of agents like students or firms. While these mechanisms are designed to be strategy-proof, agents often still attempt to manipulate the system to their advantage. This paper investigates whether agents can improve their outcomes by forming coalitions to submit joint proposals. We introduce a new concept of stability that permits such group strategy, where agents in a stable matching receive at least as good an outcome as they could achieve through any coalition. We demonstrate that stable matchings always exist and present a polynomial-time algorithm to compute them. Furthermore, we analyze the trade-off between stability and fairness, revealing that in certain scenarios, stable matchings may result in significantly worse outcomes for some agents compared to other mechanisms. Finally, we explore the computational challenges of finding stable matchings that maximize fairness. Our findings indicate that, unlike in the one-sided setting, determining stable matchings that maximize fairness is generally NP-hard. However, we also identify specific cases where these stable matchings can be found efficiently. Additionally, we examine the existence of stable matchings that are both fair and efficient, showing that such matchings do not always exist, though they can be guaranteed under certain conditions. We also discuss the computational complexity of finding these matchings when they do exist. Finally, we extend our analysis to the many-to-many setting, where agents can be matched with multiple partners simultaneously. We show that stable matchings can be computed in polynomial time in this context, and we demonstrate that stable matchings maximizing fairness always exist. These results offer a promising avenue for future research into fair and efficient resource allocation. Our work has been implemented in the open-source Python package `fairmatch`, which includes a suite of algorithms for computing various types of matchings. The package is available at https://github.com/fairmatch/fairmatch. The source code for this paper can be found at https://github.com/fairmatch/fairmatch/tree/main/papers/stable_pairing. The package also includes a tutorial on how to use it. We introduce a new approach for restoring signals from quadratic measurements, utilizing a non-convex optimization framework that is efficiently solved via a tailored alternating minimization algorithm. This method is demonstrated to restore images from highly compressed data, such as data from the Event Camera, which captures only asynchronous, asynchronous events rather than complete frames. Our approach achieves restoration quality comparable to state-of-the-art techniques while operating at least an order of magnitude faster. We validate the method's effectiveness through numerical experiments on image restoration and super-resolution tasks. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar1997/QuadraticallyObservedSignals. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive theoretical analysis of the proposed method, proving that the algorithm converges to a stationary point of the objective function within a finite number of iterations. Additionally, we establish that the algorithm recovers the true signal from a number of measurements that scales linearly with the signal's sparsity. Finally, we present a numerical study to evaluate the method's performance in image restoration and super-resolution applications. The results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms existing methods in both speed and solution quality. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 details the proposed method; Section 4 presents the theoretical analysis; and Section 5 reports numerical experiments.
