Sgr A East, a supernova remnant situated near the Galactic center, is hypothesized to have resulted from a stellar explosion that triggered the starburst activity observed in the Galactic core. This study utilizes a three-dimensional hydrodynamical simulation to investigate the impact of a supernova on the interstellar medium, specifically examining how the explosion's location influences star formation. Our findings indicate that the supernova's position is a critical factor in determining the resulting star formation rate. We demonstrate that a supernova occurring within a dense molecular cloud can generate a star formation rate of approximately 10 solar masses per year, aligning with the rate inferred from the starburst in Sgr A East. Furthermore, we show that the supernova's location dictates the morphology of the remnant, with the observed structure of Sgr A East suggesting the explosion occurred within a dense molecular cloud. These results support the hypothesis that Sgr A East originated from a supernova within a dense molecular cloud, which subsequently triggered the starburst in the Galactic center. Additionally, we explore the implications of this hypothesis for the formation of the Galactic center's massive black hole. Finally, we discuss the potential for future observations to test this hypothesis. This study presents an analysis of proton-proton collision data at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, collected by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider with an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. The search targets the non-resonant production of two Higgs bosons in association with a W or Z boson, or a top quark pair. The investigation examines various final states characterized by leptonic decays of the Higgs bosons and vector bosons, as well as decays into bottom quark pairs for the Higgs bosons and top quark pair production. Utilizing a multivariate discriminant, the analysis establishes 95% confidence level upper limits on the Higgs boson pair production cross-section, normalized to the Standard Model (SM) prediction, across a broad spectrum of Higgs boson mass combinations. These limits are derived for scenarios involving both on-shell and off-shell decays of the Higgs bosons. Furthermore, the study explores the production of two Higgs bosons with masses below 125 GeV within the framework of the Two-Higgs-Doublet Model (2HDM). In this context, the analysis focuses on the Type-II 2HDM, which is a well-motivated extension of the Standard Model. The resulting 95% confidence level upper limits on the production cross-sections for the hh and tth processes are reported as functions of the Yukawa couplings of the light and heavy Higgs bosons to bottom quarks and tau leptons. These findings are compared against the most recent direct experimental constraints. Finally, the analysis also examines the production of two Higgs bosons alongside a top quark pair. The observed upper limits on the cross-section for this process are found to be consistent with the Standard Model expectations. The corresponding limits for the ttHt process are also provided. Additionally, the study reports the first ATLAS search for Higgs boson pair production accompanied by a top quark pair, where the Higgs bosons decay into bottom quark pairs. The observed upper limits on the cross-section for this process are consistent with the Standard Model predictions. The analysis concludes with a discussion of the prospects for future searches. This study introduces a framework for assessing the fairness of machine-generated decisions within commercial driving. We examine the specific challenges inherent in evaluating such decisions and propose a solution that combines expert supervision with contextual information to ensure fair assessment. Our approach involves developing a context-aware fairness metric to evaluate expert judgments, followed by a method to automatically identify and correct inconsistencies in those decisions. We validate this framework using a real-world dataset comprising 1,000 video clips from 200 drivers, which were annotated by 100 experts. The results demonstrate that our method effectively detects and rectifies decision inconsistencies, thereby enhancing the overall fairness of the evaluation process. Furthermore, we show that this approach can significantly improve the accuracy of driver assessments. Finally, we explore the potential of our framework to facilitate the fair and accurate deployment of automated systems in commercial driving. This study examines a Gaussian stochastic field manifold (GSM) defined by a Gaussian random field (GRF) characterized by a covariance function $C(x,y)$, which is modeled as a Green's function for a linear differential operator $L$. The GSM is represented as a Riemannian manifold where the metric tensor $g_{ij}$ is determined by the covariance evaluated at the same point, $C(x,x)$. We demonstrate that the geodesic distance $D(x,y)$ on this manifold adheres to the asymptotic scaling $D(x,y) \sim |x-y|^{1-H}$, where $H$ denotes the Hurst exponent of the GRF. Furthermore, we establish that the geodesic paths within the GSM exhibit fractal characteristics, with their fractal dimension scaling as $d_f \sim 2H$. These findings are validated through numerical simulations of a specific GRF model. Additionally, we explore the potential applications of GSMs in the analysis of complex systems. Finally, we extend the analysis to random fields within the framework of random operator theory. In this context, the GSM is defined by the resolvent of the operator $L$, and we show that the geodesic distance scales as $D(x,y) \sim |x-y|^{1-\alpha}$, where $\alpha$ is the spectral exponent of the operator $L$. The fractal dimension of the geodesic paths in this scenario scales as $d_f \sim 2\alpha$. These results are also confirmed by numerical simulations. The paper concludes with a discussion of the broader implications of these findings. This work is situated within the field of stochastic geometry, which investigates the geometric properties of random sets and random fields. Specifically, it addresses the fractal nature of geodesic paths in GSMs, a topic that has received limited attention in existing literature. The results presented herein offer new insights into the geometric structure of GSMs and their potential applications in complex systems analysis. The methodology employed in this study is rigorous and well-founded, utilizing established mathematical techniques to derive the results. This paper establishes an explicit bound for the absolute value of the quotient $F/G$, where $F$ and $G$ are polynomials in $q$ arising from the factorization of $L(s, \chi, F)/L(s, \chi, G)$ for modular Dirichlet characters $\chi$. This explicit result refines the previously known bound of $O_\chi(1)$. As a consequence, we derive an explicit bound for the factors of the unique complex values of $L$-functions across all automorphic $L$-functions associated with modular forms of weight 0. Furthermore, we provide an explicit bound for the factors of the unique complex values of $L$-functions for automorphic $L$-functions of GL(n) with trivial central character. These findings are achieved by applying the explicit formula for the factors of unique values of $L$-functions of modular forms of weight 0, which was developed in our prior work. Additionally, we present an explicit bound for the factors of unique values of Hecke $L$-functions for primitive characters. The paper concludes with several applications. The first application yields an explicit bound for the absolute value of the quotient $F/G$ for modular patterns, thereby refining the $O_\chi(1)$ bound. The second application provides an explicit bound for the factors of the unique complex values of Hecke $L$-functions for primitive characters, improving upon the $O_\chi(1)$ bound. The third application offers an explicit bound for the factors of the unique complex values of $L$-functions for automorphic $L$-functions of GL(n) possessing a unitary central character, enhancing the $O_\chi(1)$ bound. Finally, the fourth application delivers an explicit bound for the factors of the unique complex values of $L$-functions for modular Dirichlet characters, refining the $O_\chi(1)$ bound. All these explicit bounds are derived by utilizing the explicit formula for the factors of unique values of $L$-functions of modular forms of weight 0. The methodology employed in this work is also applicable to deriving explicit bounds for the factors of unique complex values of Hecke $L$-functions for primitive characters. The paper concludes with an outline of the approach required to obtain these explicit bounds. The authors express gratitude to the anonymous referees for their valuable comments and suggestions. This study examines spin transport within armchair graphene nanoribbons (AGNRs) and graphene nanorings (AGNRs) featuring a central defect, specifically analyzing how the number of rings influences spin transport. Our findings indicate that the spin polarization of the current flowing through these structures is highly sensitive to the count of rings. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spin polarization of the current entering the system can be adjusted by varying the chemical potential. Additionally, we observe that the spin polarization of the current exiting the system can be modulated by altering the number of rings. These results suggest that graphene nanostructures could serve as promising candidates for spintronic applications. Finally, we conclude that the proposed model offers a viable approach for investigating spin transport in graphene nanostructures. The directed flow ($v_1$) of charged hadrons was measured in Au+Au and isobar (Ru+Ru, Zr+Zr, and $^{96,98}$Ru+$^{96,98}$Ru) collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\textrm{NN}}}=200$ GeV using the PHENIX detector at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider. The data reveal a significant mass dependence of $v_1$ at low $p_{\textrm{T}}$, which remains consistent with prior findings. Furthermore, the mass dependence of $v_1$ exhibits a marked variation with collision system mass, a feature that is well-described by viscous hydrodynamic models incorporating a shear viscosity-to-entropy density ratio of $\eta/s=0.12$. Additionally, the directed flow of hadrons in these collisions displays a strong dependence on the number of protons ($N_p$) within the participating nucleons. This $N_p$ dependence is also accurately reproduced by viscous hydrodynamic simulations. The observed directed flow of hadrons in these collisions is well-explained by the initial spatial anisotropy of the quark-gluon plasma, as predicted by the initial geometry of the collisions. These findings offer valuable insights into the characteristics of the quark-gluon plasma and the transport properties of the medium created in heavy-ion collisions. This study introduces a new sparse-grid-driven adaptive spectral Koopman method designed for identifying low-dimensional invariant manifolds within nonlinear dynamical systems. The approach utilizes sparse-grid-based spectral k-extrapolation to construct a nonlinear operator that maps functions defined on the system's state space to their corresponding Koopman images. By employing a greedy algorithm, the method adaptively refines the sampling set to enhance the accuracy of these Koopman images. Furthermore, it leverages the spectral properties of the nonlinear operator to generate an initial estimate of the invariant manifold, which serves as the foundation for a subsequent spectral analysis. The technique's efficacy is demonstrated through its application to a nonlinear pendulum and a nonlinear oscillator. Additionally, the paper provides a theoretical analysis of the method's convergence and error estimates. Finally, the proposed approach is validated using a nonlinear dynamical system derived from the Navier-Stokes equations. The results indicate that the method achieves high accuracy in modeling the system's dynamics and effectively captures the dominant modes of the system. These findings underscore the potential of the sparse-grid-driven adaptive spectral Koopman technique for analyzing complex nonlinear dynamical systems. This study introduces a new approach to solving the time-independent Schrödinger equation for atoms and molecules under strong direct-current (DC) electric fields. By applying complex scaling to the radial coordinate outward from the origin, we derive a complex scaled Hamiltonian that yields complex eigenvalues. The real component of these eigenvalues corresponds to the energy levels, while the imaginary component relates to the state's lifetime. We demonstrate that this method produces accurate eigenvalues for hydrogen atoms and molecules across a broad spectrum of DC field strengths. Furthermore, we show that the technique remains effective even when the DC field is strong enough to induce significant ionization. Finally, we illustrate that the method can be extended to include AC fields. These findings indicate that the proposed approach offers a versatile and efficient framework for investigating atoms and molecules in intense electromagnetic fields. Additionally, the method holds potential for exploring other phenomena, such as Stark resonances and Stark ionization rates. The Sinkhorn algorithm is a well-established iterative technique for resolving the Schr\"odinger problem, which involves computing a solution matrix that simultaneously row and column scales a nonnegative matrix to match prescribed row and column sums. This study examines the Sinkhorn algorithm's behavior when applied to matrices for which no solution exists. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the algorithm converges to a solution for the Schr\"odingr problem involving an infinite number of constraints. Furthermore, we establish convergence to a solution for the related problem of scaling a nonnegative matrix to achieve a specified row sum profile, even in scenarios where no solution exists. Finally, we present numerical examples illustrating the algorithm's performance in cases where it fails to converge. These findings are derived from a novel approach to analyzing the Sinkhorn algorithm, which utilizes the theory of monotone operators. This method offers a fresh perspective on the algorithm's convergence properties. Additionally, we provide a concise overview of the monotone operator framework and its application to the Sinkhorn algorithm, with the aim of making this methodology accessible to a broader audience. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the monotone operator theory and its utility in analyzing the Sinkhorn algorithm; Section 3 addresses the case where a solution exists; Section 4 explores the scenario where a solution does not exist; and Section 5 concludes with a discussion of open questions. The pandemic has significantly altered human interaction patterns, a change that has been quantified through urban interaction networks. This study examines the disparity in these interactions across different income levels within the United States. By analyzing the pandemic's impact on interaction behavior, we observed that the disparity in urban interactions intensified during this period. Specifically, the income-based gap in interactions increased by 1.5 times compared to pre-pandemic levels. This disparity is primarily driven by the fact that individuals with higher incomes engaged in more outdoor activities, whereas those with lower incomes participated in fewer such activities. Furthermore, we found that the pandemic's effect on income disparity was more pronounced in densely populated areas. These findings underscore the necessity of implementing targeted policies to mitigate the exacerbation of income inequality in urban interactions caused by the pandemic. Additionally, they highlight the critical role of urban planning in fostering social equity. Finally, our results demonstrate that the proposed framework can effectively capture the behavioral shifts induced by the pandemic. This study evaluates the performance of nonlinear field-split preconditioners within a fully implicit two-phase flow simulator, specifically targeting heterogeneous porous media characterized by high permeability contrasts. The analysis focuses on two distinct scenarios: a 1D heterogeneous core flood and a 2D heterogeneous reservoir model. The paper details the methodology for constructing nonlinear field-split preconditioners and compares them against a standard Schur complement preconditioner. Results indicate that the nonlinear field-split approach achieves faster convergence rates than the Schur complement method in both test cases. Furthermore, the study examines the impact of varying permeability contrasts and capillary numbers on convergence speed, concluding that the nonlinear field-split preconditioner remains effective across a broad spectrum of these parameters. Finally, the influence of grid size on convergence is assessed, demonstrating that the preconditioner performs well across a range of grid sizes. Overall, the research confirms that the nonlinear field-split preconditioner is highly effective for simulating two-phase flow in heterogeneous porous media. We introduce a novel design for chiral optical cavities featuring unilateral light-matter interaction. This mechanism relies on a single atom positioned within a dielectric wedge, where the atom's position is optimized to ensure that only one of its transition dipoles couples with the cavity mode. We demonstrate that this design achieves a high degree of chiral coupling, reaching up to 99.9%. Furthermore, we show that the unilateral interaction can be toggled on and off by adjusting the atom's position. Finally, we explore potential applications of this system, including chiral quantum networks, the generation of chiral single-photon sources, and the realization of non-reciprocal devices. These findings establish a foundation for developing new photonic components and devices. Additionally, we outline a feasible experimental approach to implement this proposal using existing technology. In contrast, for the Liouville CFT, we establish that the bound is not saturated. Furthermore, we analyze the Liouville CFT partition function on a disk using a matrix model and show that this bound is likewise not saturated within that framework. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the holographic bound. We introduce a method to investigate the thermal characteristics of a two-dimensional ion crystal by monitoring spin dephasing as ions are progressively heated. This approach enables the measurement of thermal energy, heating rates, and the full width at half maximum of the vibrational mode distribution. By analyzing spin dephasing, we can determine the participation of individual ions in collective motion and identify the specific ions constituting the crystal's surface. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ion crystal's surface is not rigid; instead, surface ions can be ejected into the vacuum, and these ions can be reintegrated into the crystal. This methodology is applicable to any trapped-ion system, offering a versatile tool for characterizing the thermal properties of trapped ions. Our findings are consistent with a heating model where the ions behave as a classical solid. Additionally, we observe that the heating rate increases as the ion count decreases, a phenomenon that may be attributed to the reduced efficiency of sympathetic cooling. These results hold significant implications for the development of large-scale trapped-ion quantum computers. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending this technique to three-dimensional ion crystals. This research was conducted using the trapped-ion quantum simulator at the University of Maryland. Our findings indicate that both subpar and characteristic RL strategies correlate with the midbrain's encoding of prediction errors. These results support the notion that the midbrain plays a pivotal role in RL by signaling the timing of value updates. Additionally, we show that the striatum encodes the temporal dynamics of subpar RL, whereas the hippocampus encodes those of characteristic RL. These results suggest that the striatum and hippocampus contribute differently to RL, with the former facilitating value updates and the latter enabling the learning of task structure. Finally, we demonstrate that the midbrain's encoding of prediction errors is robust to variations in the task's temporal structure. The approach models the imaging process as a linear operator acting on material density maps, which are subsequently regularized using a data-driven total variation (TV) norm. To address sensor noise, the framework incorporates a data fidelity term that minimizes the discrepancy between observed noisy data and the forward projection of these density maps. The optimization problem is solved via an alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), yielding a closed-form solution for each iteration. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves superior noise suppression and material decomposition accuracy compared to existing techniques. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness against data noise and effectively handles low-dose CT scenarios. Finally, the computational efficiency of the proposed approach is evaluated. This study examines how electron spill-over and nonlocality influence gap-plasmon resonances in the limit of vanishing gaps. We demonstrate that electron spill-over causes a redshift in the resonance, whereas nonlocality results in a blueshift. Furthermore, we find that the magnitude of the redshift induced by spill-over increases as the gap approaches zero, while the magnitude of the shift caused by nonlocality diminishes in this limit. These findings are derived from numerical solutions to the Maxwell equations and the quantum hydrodynamic model. Additionally, we show that the resonance shift due to electron spill-over can be accurately predicted using a simple analytical model. Finally, we analyze the resonance shift for a system of two half-spaces separated by a dielectric layer of thickness $d$, illustrating that the shift scales with the gap size as $d^2$ when the gap is small. This scaling behavior is independent of the specific materials involved. We also provide an analytical explanation for this result. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for experimental observations. Our results indicate that the resonance shift caused by electron spill-over is negligible for gaps larger than approximately 1 nm, but becomes significant for gaps smaller than 0.5 nm. In contrast, the resonance shift due to nonlocality is significant for gaps smaller than approximately 0.1 nm. These conclusions are based on the assumption that the gap is filled with a dielectric material. However, if the gap is filled with a metal, the resonance shift due to nonlocality is expected to be larger than in the dielectric case. This is because the nonlocality of the metal's dielectric function is more pronounced at the frequencies where the gap-plasmon resonance occurs. We also discuss the implications of these findings for the design of nanophotonic devices. While recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled the extraction of structured information from DHRs, these data are often stored in silos, making cross-organization analysis difficult. This study examines the electric double layer (EDL) adjacent to a charged soft interface within an electrolyte solution, incorporating solvent polarization effects. We derive an analytical solution for the Poisson-Boltzmann equation, which includes a nonlinear term representing solvent polarization, under the assumption of a Gaussian distribution of counterions within the polymer layer. Our findings indicate that solvent polarization significantly alters the potential distribution and the thickness of the EDL. Furthermore, we observe that these effects are more pronounced in electrolytes with lower valency. Finally, we demonstrate that the impact of solvent polarization on the EDL is substantially greater at the molecular scale than at the continuum scale. These results underscore the critical role of solvent polarization in governing the electrostatic properties of soft interfaces. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive discussion of the model's limitations and potential avenues for future research. The paper concludes with a summary of the key findings. Software requirements serve as the foundation for developing and maintaining software systems, yet they are frequently absent, outdated, or poorly documented. This paper introduces a method for automatically generating software specifications from unstructured textual sources. The approach leverages a large corpus of domain-specific documents to learn a statistical model that transforms unstructured text into structured requirements. X-ray absorption edge spectroscopy (XAS) is a widely used method for investigating the electronic and local structural characteristics of materials. Although XAS is typically analyzed using linear models, non-linear effects emerge at high fluences, complicating data interpretation. This study introduces a rate equation framework to model the time-dependent populations of electronic states during XAS experiments. The resulting theoretical predictions align closely with experimental data, and the model's parameters can be derived from first principles. Furthermore, this approach offers a pathway to mitigate non-linear artifacts in high-fluence XAS measurements. The proposed rate equation formalism is also applicable to other spectroscopic techniques that induce non-linear electronic state populations. We introduce a novel algorithm designed to compute dual comparison, a problem that involves determining whether the optimal values of two distinct optimization problems align on a specific input. This issue encompasses several significant problems in database theory, including conjunctive query containment, universal cover containment, and conjunctive containment. Our method relies on a new concept termed a "dual homomorphism," which is defined through a linear program. We demonstrate that this linear program can be resolved in polynomial time for a broad category of comparison problems. Furthermore, we establish that for certain specific instances, such as query containment, our algorithm is optimal. Finally, we present a comprehensive classification of the computational complexity for dual comparison across various database problems. Notably, we identify a new database problem, dual reachability, which is provably harder than query containment. Additionally, we provide a complete complexity classification for dual reachability and prove that its containment problem is NP-complete. Our findings indicate that the proposed algorithm is optimal for dual reachability containment. The paper concludes with a discussion on the limitations of our approach and potential avenues for future research. We introduce a novel PopSyCLE simulation designed to investigate the formation of primordial black holes (PBHs) as dark matter, specifically within the mass range of $10^{-16}$ to $10^{-10}$ solar masses. This simulation tracks the evolution of PBHs from the radiation-dominated era through to the present day, incorporating accretion physics and the impact of cosmic expansion on their number density. Our results indicate that PBHs can account for dark matter if their mass falls between $10^{-16}$ and $10^{-15}$ solar masses. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dark energy density of the universe can be explained by PBHs with masses ranging from $10^{-15}$ to $10^{-10}$ solar masses, provided they are produced during the matter-dominated era. Finally, we compare our findings with existing observational constraints. Our analysis reveals that the PBH dark energy model is viable only if the PBH mass function is highly peaked, as a broad distribution would result in a significant fraction of PBHs falling into the mass range required for dark matter. Additionally, we find that the PBH dark energy model is incompatible with the observed lack of gamma-ray bursts from accreting black holes. However, this discrepancy can be resolved if PBHs are not distributed homogeneously throughout the universe. We conclude that future observations of gamma-ray bursts and the cosmic microwave background will be essential for testing the PBH dark energy hypothesis. Our study demonstrates that PBHs can serve as dark matter, dark energy, or both, contingent upon their mass and formation epoch. This paper examines the challenge of determining the most preferred set from a collection of existing sets, where a new element is to be added. The resulting set is anticipated to be preferred over any of the original ones. We analyze this problem within both non-contextual and contextual frameworks. In the non-contextual scenario, we demonstrate that the problem is NP-hard and that no polynomial-time approximation algorithm exists unless P equals NP. Conversely, in the contextual setting, we establish that the problem can be solved in polynomial time. Furthermore, we explore the connections between this task and the maximum weight independent set problem. Finally, we present experimental results comparing our proposed algorithms against a baseline approach. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robin-berthier/Preference-Set-Addition.

This study examines the thermodynamic and dynamic properties of a glass-forming polymer liquid across a broad temperature range, utilizing both experimental data and molecular dynamics simulations. The findings reveal that the relationship between enthalpy and structural relaxation time remains linear, a characteristic that persists even when the system is cooled well below the glass transition temperature. Furthermore, the activation energy for relaxation is determined to be 1.1 eV, a value consistent with the polymer's cohesive energy. These results indicate that the thermodynamic and dynamic behaviors of this glass-forming liquid are governed by the same energy scale. Consequently, the thermodynamic state of the liquid can be defined by a single variable, and the thermodynamic framework for glass-forming liquids is extended to encompass the glassy state. Finally, the observed linear correlation between enthalpy and relaxation time is interpreted as evidence for the potential energy landscape of the glass-forming liquid. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these results for the fundamental understanding of glass formation. We report on a comprehensive investigation into the diffuse gamma-ray background (DGRB) generated by galaxy clusters. Utilizing the most recent data from the Planck satellite, we identify 1,000 clusters with redshifts below 0.1, which we designate as the Planck-1k sample. By applying a novel method to estimate the X-ray luminosity of these clusters, we calculate the expected gamma-ray flux from their inverse Compton scattering (ICS) emission. Our results indicate that the Planck-1k sample alone accounts for approximately 10% of the DGRB, a figure that rises to 20% when including clusters with redshifts up to 0.2. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ICS signal from the Planck-1k sample is detectable by the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) at a 3-sigma confidence level. Finally, we show that the ICS signal from the Planck-1k sample can be distinguished from the DGRB by the upcoming CTA observatory with a significance exceeding 10 sigma. These findings suggest that the ICS signal from galaxy clusters represents a substantial fraction of the DGRB, a conclusion that is further supported by the detection of the ICS signal from the Coma cluster by CTA. Consequently, our results underscore the critical importance of studying the ICS signal from galaxy clusters for both current and future gamma-ray observatories. We demonstrate that the coupling between phonons and electrons generates a long-range attractive interaction between electrons in one-dimensional cuprates. This attraction arises from the phonon-mediated exchange of virtual phonons, a mechanism that is particularly strong when the phonon dispersion is flat. Consequently, this effect is most pronounced in the CuO$_2$ planes of cuprates, where the electronic band structure exhibits flat dispersions. This finding offers a potential explanation for the observed long-range attractive interactions in these materials. Furthermore, we show that this interaction can induce a phase transition from a Luttinger liquid to a charge density wave state. Finally, we predict that this phenomenon can be experimentally verified through Raman spectroscopy. Our results suggest that phonon-mediated interactions may play a crucial role in the physics of cuprates. Additionally, we propose that materials with flat dispersions, such as cuprates, could serve as promising platforms for studying phonon-mediated interactions. This study underscores the significance of incorporating flat dispersions into theoretical models of cuprates. The metastable body-centered tetragonal (bct) phase of Co$_{9}$Zn$_{9}$Mn$_{2}$ exhibits a skyrmion lattice (SkL) at low temperatures and low magnetic fields. By employing in situ small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) and magnetic force microscopy (MFM), we demonstrate that the bct SkL undergoes a first-order geometric melting transition into a face-centered tetragonal (fct) SkL at a critical field $H_{c}$. This process is driven by the reorientation of the easy axis from the $c$-direction to the $a$-direction. We show that this geometric melting can be bypassed by substituting Co with Ni, which stabilizes the fct SkL at low fields. Furthermore, we observe that the fct SkL undergoes a second first-order transition into a disordered state at a critical field $H_{d}$, which is significantly lower than the melting field of the bct SkL. This behavior is attributed to the reduced anisotropy in the Ni-containing alloy. Finally, we discuss the potential for utilizing this geometric melting mechanism to generate topological defects. These findings offer new insights into the physics of topological defects and their applications in spintronics. Additionally, the observed first-order transition from the bct to the fct SkL represents a novel topological phase transition. The balance problem seeks to identify a stable configuration of $n$ points within a domain under the influence of both pairwise repulsive forces and an attractive force directed toward a fixed point. This study examines the balance problem in two dimensions, where the repulsive force between points $p$ and $q$ is defined as $|p-q|^{-\alpha}$ and the attractive force as $|p-o|^{-\beta}$, with $\alpha, \beta \in (0,2)$ and $o$ located at the origin. We establish the existence of a stable configuration within any bounded domain and demonstrate that, for any $\alpha, \beta \in (0,2)$, a stable configuration exists in the entire plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ provided the domain of attraction of the origin is bounded. Furthermore, we prove that if $\alpha \in (0,2)$ and $\beta \in [2,4)$, the set of stable configurations in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is non-empty and compact. Finally, we show that for $\alpha, \beta \in (0,2)$, the set of stable configurations in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is non-empty whenever the origin is a local minimizer of the potential energy function. Additionally, we derive a lower bound for the cardinality of this set when $\alpha, \beta \in (0,2)$. These findings are achieved by analyzing the stability of configurations where all points share the same distance from the origin. The methodology employed involves a novel approach to the balance problem, termed the "stable point approach," which utilizes a continuous-time dynamical system to investigate the stability of such configurations. This approach is applicable to balance problems in both two and three dimensions. Finally, we present numerical results for the case where $\alpha=1$ and $\beta=2$. The paper concludes with a discussion of open questions. This work extends the findings of [10] and [11] from dimensions $d \geq 3$ to $d=2$. The primary distinction between the $d=2$ case and higher dimensions lies in the behavior of the potential energy function at infinity. Specifically, in $\mathbb{R}^d$ for $d \geq 3$, the potential energy function is bounded from below, whereas in $\mathbb{R}^2$, it is bounded from below only under the condition $\alpha+\beta \geq 2$.

Dimuonium ($\mu^+\mu^-$) is a bound state of two muons, which can be generated in high-energy particle collisions. This study introduces MuMuPy, a computational tool designed to calculate the energy shifts and decay widths of dimuonium arising from its interactions with external fields and matter. The program is validated by reproducing the known $2S$ hydrogen-like atom energy spectrum and by estimating the dimuonium decay width, which aligns with prior literature. MuMuPy is implemented in Python and is accessible at https://github.com/andrewjamesg/mumupy. This tool is intended to support experimental and phenomenological investigations into dimuonium decays and its interactions with external environments. Furthermore, MuMuPy can be utilized to determine the muon magnetic moment by analyzing the hyperfine splitting of the dimuonium ground state. The program is also applicable to muonium (bound $\mu^+e^-$) and positronium (bound $e^+e^-$) systems. The authors anticipate that MuMuPy will facilitate the determination of the muon magnetic moment with a precision of $10^{-10}$, thereby enabling a stringent test of the Standard Model. This level of precision is necessary to resolve the current $3.7\sigma$ discrepancy between the $(g-2)_\mu$ value derived from the Muon $g-2$ experiment and the theoretical prediction. The tool is also relevant to the proposed Muonium Quantum Simulator (MQS) initiative, which aims to explore fundamental physics questions, including the nature of dark matter. The authors hope that MuMuPy will assist in advancing the MQS project. Additionally, the program can be employed to investigate the possibility of dimuonium formation within the early universe. The paper concludes with a discussion of the limitations of MuMuPy. The source code is available at https://github.com/andrewjamesg/mumupy. This work is dedicated to the memory of Professor John L. This study examines a single-period investment framework where an investor allocates wealth between a risk-free asset and a single risky asset. The investor's objective is to maximize the expected utility of a linear combination of absolute and relative wealth, with the relative component defined as the ratio of terminal wealth to that of a benchmark. We derive the closed-form solution for the optimal investment strategy under power utility functions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the optimal allocation to the risky asset remains constant over time and is independent of the investor's risk aversion parameter. Finally, we provide a numerical analysis to illustrate the impact of various parameters on relative wealth. These findings offer valuable insights for investors seeking to balance the trade-off between absolute and relative wealth performance. Hydrogen Lyman-$\alpha$ emission from the intergalactic medium (IGM) surrounding dwarf galaxies serves as a critical indicator of their IGM properties. This study examines the observational characteristics of this emission, its theoretical underpinnings, and its implications for the physical state of the IGM around these galaxies. We analyze the spatial distribution of Lyman-$\alpha$ halos around the Local Group dwarfs, specifically focusing on the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds (SMC and LMC). Our findings indicate that the SMC and LMC possess extended Lyman-$\alpha$ halos extending approximately 100 kpc, with a mean surface brightness of $10^{-17}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ arcsec$^{-2}$ at 10 kpc. We compare these observations with predictions from photoionization models, which suggest that the IGM around these galaxies is highly ionized, with a mean electron density of $10^{-4}$ cm$^{-3}$ and a temperature of 10,000 K. Furthermore, we explore the potential for detecting Lyman-$\alpha$ halos around other Local Group dwarfs and discuss the broader significance of these observations for understanding the IGM. Finally, we address the implications of these results for the IGM around galaxies at high redshifts. Our analysis suggests that Lyman-$\alpha$ halos around high-redshift galaxies may be more luminous than previously estimated, potentially reaching $10^{-16}$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$ arcsec$^{-2}$ at 10 kpc. This finding could aid in the identification of Lyman-$\alpha$ emitters and facilitate the study of the IGM around high-redshift galaxies. Additionally, we propose that the observed Lyman-$\alpha$ halos around the SMC and LMC could serve as a probe for the IGM's physical properties, such as density and temperature, during the epoch of reionization. This approach could offer valuable insights into the IGM's evolution and its role in the formation and evolution of galaxies. Ultimately, our results underscore the significance of Lyman-$\alpha$ halos around galaxies as a vital tool for investigating the IGM and its influence on galaxy formation and evolution. By studying these halos, we can gain a deeper understanding of the IGM's physical properties and its impact on the development of galaxies throughout cosmic history

This study investigates the variability in performance among Mechanical Turk (MTurk) crowdworkers, specifically within the domain of summarization. Our findings indicate that while task design can facilitate the detection of qualified performers, it does not guarantee their identification. Furthermore, we observe that workers' performance is highly dependent on the specific topic of the task. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for the broader field of crowdsourcing. However, this approach often fails to capture the nuanced relationships between text tokens and video frames, leading to suboptimal retrieval performance. To address these limitations, we introduce TS2-Net, a novel network that incorporates a token shift mechanism to model interactions between text tokens and video frames. This paper examines a directed hybrid random network that integrates the preferential attachment and uniform attachment mechanisms. In this model, a new node connects to an existing one with a probability proportional to the target node's in-degree, while the remaining probability is used to attach to a randomly selected node. We analyze the asymptotic behavior of the in-degree distribution for this hybrid model. Our findings indicate that the in-degree distribution converges to a power-law distribution with an exponent of 3 when the attachment probability is proportional to in-degree, and to a geometric distribution when the probability is constant. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the distribution of the attachment probability itself follows a beta distribution. Additionally, we prove that the model exhibits the small-world property, meaning the average path length between any two nodes grows logarithmically with the network size. Finally, we validate these theoretical results through numerical simulations. The code used to generate the figures is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/Paper-20210211. A measure algebra is defined as locally normal if its associated measure space admits a system of normal measures that is closed under countable unions. This paper demonstrates that every locally normal measure algebra possesses a complete atomless Boolean subalgebra capable of generating the entire algebra. Furthermore, the existence of a locally normal measure algebra with a complete, atomless Boolean subalgebra that fails to be locally normal is established. The study also examines the relationship between locally normal measure algebras and those that are $\sigma$-decomposable. Finally, the paper investigates the properties of locally normal measure algebras within the context of forcing. Specifically, it is proven that if $N$ is a locally normal measure algebra and $R$ is a complete atomless Boolean algebra, then the tensor product $N\otimes R$ remains locally normal. Additionally, the tensor product of two locally normal measure algebras is shown to be locally normal under the assumption of the Proper Forcing Axiom (PFA). However, the consistency of the existence of a locally normal measure algebra whose tensor product with itself is not locally normal is also established. The paper concludes by exploring the connection between locally normal measure algebras and the existence of a nontrivial $\sigma$-decomposable normal measure on a complete atomless Boolean algebra. It is demonstrated that the existence of such a measure is equivalent to the existence of a locally normal measure algebra that possesses a $\sigma$-decomposable normal measure which is not contained within any complete atomless Boolean subalgebra. Finally, it is noted that the existence of a locally normal measure algebra with a $\sigma$-decomposable normal measure is consistent with the Proper Forcing Axiom. We present a theoretical investigation into the thermal evolution of the superfluid order parameter within an optical lattice, specifically for bosons exhibiting spin-orbit coupling. Our analysis reveals that thermal fluctuations induce a shift in the modulation wave vector of the superfluid order parameter, a phenomenon that intensifies with increasing coupling strength. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this shift can be mitigated by adjusting the ratio of inter- to intra-site interactions. Finally, we establish that the magnitude of this wave vector shift serves as a reliable indicator of the spin-orbit coupling strength. These findings are derived from a theoretical framework combining the large-$U$ expansion with the self-consistent Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov method. Additionally, we show that the proposed approach accurately reproduces the thermal evolution of the momentum distribution for spin-orbit-coupled bosons in an optical lattice, as obtained from exact diagonalization. This suggests that our method is applicable to a broad spectrum of strongly correlated bosonic systems. Our results offer a quantitative prediction of the impact of spin-orbit coupling on the thermal evolution of the superfluid order parameter, a prediction that can be experimentally verified using ultracold atoms in optical lattices. Such verification would provide a valuable tool for characterizing spin-orbit coupling in ultracold atomic systems. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending this approach to other relevant systems, including those involving spin-orbit-coupled fermions and spinful fermions subject to strong correlations. Additionally, we establish an upper bound for the degradation number of such Cayley graphs and demonstrate that this bound is tight. Furthermore, we derive an upper limit for the structural degradation number of these graphs, proving that this limit is also sharp. Finally, we present an algorithm to determine the structural degradation number for any given graph. The performance of this algorithm is validated through several illustrative examples. In this study, a graph $G$ is defined as realized by a group if $G$ is isomorphic to a Cayley graph of that group. The degradation number of a graph $G$ represents the minimum count of edges required to be removed from $G$ so that the resulting graph lacks a Cayley representation. The structural degradation number refers to the minimum number of edges that must be removed from $G$ to ensure the new graph is not isomorphic to any Cayley graph. Consequently, the structural degradation number is invariant under graph isomorphism. Beam-induced coherent synchrotron radiation (BCSR) and beam breakup (BBU) pose significant threats to the stable operation of muon colliders. This paper examines various strategies to suppress these effects, including the use of low-impedance cavities, muon cooling, and the optimization of muon beam parameters. Additionally, we explore the potential for utilizing BCSR as a diagnostic tool to measure muon beam density. The proposed mitigation techniques are evaluated through numerical simulations. Our findings indicate that BCSR and BBU can be effectively managed in muon colliders, provided that the muon beam density remains sufficiently low. Furthermore, we demonstrate that BCSR-induced noise is more readily suppressed than BBU-induced noise. Finally, we establish that the maximum achievable muon beam density is primarily determined by the BBU effect. These conclusions are derived from a comprehensive analysis of the underlying physics. We anticipate that this study will offer valuable insights for the design of future muon collider facilities. This work is dedicated to the memory of Professor John D. Jackson. We introduce Spartan, a method that optimizes neural network weights to achieve sparsity by minimizing a conveyance regularizer. This regularizer penalizes the deviation of the network's output from its average behavior across the input batch, thereby promoting sparsity through regularized conveyance. We demonstrate that Spartan converges to a sparse solution when the conveyance regularizer is sufficiently strong. Furthermore, we establish that Spartan is differentiable, enabling the use of gradient descent for optimization. Experimental results on image classification benchmarks indicate that Spartan produces sparse models with competitive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we show that Spartan can be integrated with other sparsity methods, such as Lasso, to enhance their performance. Finally, we confirm that Spartan is capable of generating sparse models suitable for deployment on edge devices. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/Spartan. We demonstrate that an emergent Pauli obstruction arises within the one-dimensional Bose-Hubbard model even at weak interaction strengths, provided the ratio between nearest-neighbor hopping and next-nearest-neighbor hopping is a rational number. This phenomenon is linked to the existence of a macroscopic ground state with zero momentum. We establish that this Pauli-like behavior persists in the continuum limit of the Bose gas, contingent upon the fulfillment of specific boundary conditions. Furthermore, we show that this emergent Pauli obstruction can be eliminated by introducing a sufficiently strong three-body interaction. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the realization of a one-dimensional Bose-Einstein condensate within the fractional quantum Hall regime. These results are derived using a combination of exact diagonalization, density-matrix renormalization group, and analytical methods. Additionally, we present experimental data from a one-dimensional Bose gas, confirming the emergence of this Pauli-like behavior in the weakly interacting regime. The observed phenomenon is attributed to the formation of a macroscopic zero-momentum state, which is facilitated by the application of specific boundary conditions. This study highlights the significant role of boundary conditions in the formation of Bose-Einstein condensates. Our findings offer a novel pathway to explore the interplay between Pauli and Bose statistics in one-dimensional Bose gases. Test smells are recognized as indicators of deeper issues within the testing process, yet their severity has not been thoroughly investigated. This study examines the perspectives of software developers on how serious test smells are. Data was gathered through an online survey of 100 developers, who ranked the smells from most to least severe. The findings reveal that 60% of participants consider at least one test smell to be severe. Furthermore, the smells identified as most serious include "test duplication," "test code in production code," and "tests that are too slow." These results offer valuable insights for developers, managers, and researchers, highlighting the need to address test duplication and the entanglement of test and production code. Additionally, the study provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of test smell research. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. This study introduces the Monte Carlo event generator \texttt{KKMcee}, which calculates the production of lepton and quark pairs in electron-positron collisions, incorporating both initial- and final-state radiation. The process is modeled up to the second order in the electromagnetic coupling, with photon radiation handled to the third order in the electromagnetic charge. Beyond the primary hard process, the simulation also includes the decay of heavy quarkonium states into diphotons and gluons. Numerical results are presented for the $Z$ boson, Higgs boson, and quarkonium production. Furthermore, the paper provides an overview of the simulation capabilities for the $\Upsilon(1S)$ decay into diphotons and gluons. This paper introduces a novel method for estimating inter-beat intervals (IBI) using the Tiramisu model, which is designed to capture the periodic nature of IBI data. The study demonstrates that the Tiramisu model effectively extracts features from raw IBI signals, yielding superior results compared to other models. Furthermore, the authors show that the model's performance is highly sensitive to the selection of hyper-parameters. Finally, the paper highlights the significant impact of the training dataset on the model's accuracy. Experimental findings indicate that the Tiramisu model achieves a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.011 seconds and a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.014 seconds when trained on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database. Additionally, the model successfully detects heartbeats in the MIT-BIH Atrial Fibrillation Database with an accuracy of 99.99%. These results confirm that the Tiramisu model is highly effective for IBI assessment. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/AbdulRahman12345/Tiramisu. The ground state of $^7$H is investigated as a cluster system composed of $^3$H and four neutrons. The study examines the influence of the $^3$H core on the binding energy and the spatial distribution of the neutrons. Furthermore, the $^7$H+$p$ reaction is analyzed to explore the formation of the $^3$H+4n configuration. The findings indicate that the binding energy of the $^3$H+4n excitation is approximately 0.5 MeV, and the neutrons are distributed in a diffuse manner. Additionally, the $^7$H+$p$ reaction exhibits a strong preference for the $^3$H+4n excitation, with a calculated cross section of roughly 10 mb. These results suggest that the $^7$H ground state can be effectively described as a $^3$H+4n excitation. The methodology employed is applicable to other exotic nuclei. Finally, the potential for using the $^7$H+$p$ reaction to investigate the $^3$H+4n excitation is discussed. This study evaluates how local tracing collaborations affect the efficiency of contact tracing for COVID-19 in England. We utilized a dataset of 1,000,000 cases from the first year of the pandemic, analyzing the impact of these collaborations on case notification times and the proportion of cases successfully traced. Our findings indicate that while tracing collaborations reduced notification times, they did not significantly alter the overall effectiveness of case notification or tracing. Furthermore, we observed that the effectiveness of case notification and tracing varied across different regions of England. Finally, we demonstrated that the effectiveness of case notification is highly sensitive to the assumed distribution of incubation periods. These results suggest that the current contact tracing system in England is not sufficiently effective to serve as the primary intervention for controlling the pandemic. Instead, the system should be viewed as a supplementary measure to other interventions, such as vaccination, to help mitigate the spread of the virus. Additionally, we recommend that future research incorporate more realistic assumptions regarding incubation periods and the timing of symptom onset. This paper investigates the topological characteristics of Gaussian wandering sets within real analytic families of functions, specifically focusing on sparse polynomials. We establish that, with high probability, the wandering sets associated with linear sections of these functions exhibit a trivial homology structure. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the total Betti numbers of the wandering sets across the entire function family are bounded by a constant. These findings are applicable to both real and complex domains. Additionally, we extend our results to a broader class of functions, encompassing those that are not necessarily sparse. The methodology employed relies on a novel approach to analyzing the topology of Gaussian wandering sets, which may hold independent significance. Finally, we present several applications of these theoretical results. We introduce a vertex divider that, given a graph with bounded treewidth, partitions the graph into two roughly equal halves by removing only a minimal number of vertices. This divider is derived from a tree decomposition and can be identified in linear time. Our findings are particularly significant for graphs with treewidth $w$ and $n$ vertices, where the count of deleted vertices scales as $O(n/w)$. This represents an exponential improvement over prior methods, which required removing $O(n/2^w)$ vertices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the problem of determining the minimum cut in treewidth-bounded graphs is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the treewidth. Additionally, we establish that the problem of partitioning a graph into two equal halves by removing the fewest possible vertices is NP-hard, even when the graph possesses bounded treewidth. Finally, we present a fixed-parameter algorithm capable of computing a vertex divider with $O(n/w)$ deleted vertices for graphs with treewidth $w$ in $2^{O(w^2)}n^{O(1)}$ time. This approach surpasses the best-known algorithms for the related graph separator problem, which operate in $2^{O(w^2)}n$ time. Our techniques are applicable to a broad class of problems that can be solved using tree decompositions. We illustrate this by applying our methods to the maximum independent set problem, achieving a running time of $2^{O(w^2)}n^{O(1)}$, which is superior to the best existing bounds. This result also improves upon the fastest known algorithm for the more general vertex cover problem. The primary technical advancement enabling these results is a novel method for identifying a tree decomposition that is nearly optimal in size. This method is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the treewidth and can be executed in $2^{O(w^2)}n^{O(1)}$ time. Our approach is based on a dynamic programming algorithm that utilizes a recursive characterization of treewidth. We anticipate that this algorithm will prove valuable for other applications involving tree decompositions. The paper includes a detailed analysis of the algorithm's running time. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the algorithm can be adapted to construct a tree decomposition that is nearly optimal in size. This decomposition can be computed in $2^{O(w^2)}n^{O(1)}$ time and serves as the foundation for our vertex divider. The algorithm also yields a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for the graph separator problem, which was previously known to be fixed-parameter tractable.

We introduce a tunneling spectroscopy technique utilizing resistive electrodes to identify the Majorana peak and differentiate it from other peaks. This approach is applicable to systems exhibiting Ohmic damping, such as those formed by a superconductor-semiconductor nanowire junction or a topological Josephson junction. The proposed method offers a straightforward and effective means of detecting the Majorana peak. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this technique can identify the Majorana peak even in the presence of disorder. Our findings indicate that the tunneling conductance peaks exhibit a linear dependence on the bias voltage, a characteristic that distinguishes them from Andreev bound state peaks. Additionally, we show that the conductance peaks display a linear relationship with the tunneling resistance, a feature that further separates them from Andreev bound state peaks. Finally, we illustrate that the tunneling conductance peaks remain robust against variations in the tunneling resistance, the chemical potential, and the strength of the disorder. These results suggest that the tunneling conductance peaks are highly promising for the detection of Majorana zero modes. This paper introduces a reinforcement learning framework designed to investigate how data contamination impacts GNNs. We demonstrate that even minor levels of contamination can severely impair model performance, with the extent of degradation varying significantly across different graph datasets. Furthermore, we find that the effectiveness of a GNN in resisting contamination is largely determined by the specific graph structure. Our experimental results indicate that reinforcement learning offers a promising approach for analyzing the consequences of data contamination within these networks. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive discussion of the study's limitations and outline potential avenues for future research. This study examines the Soret effect in a binary mixture of hard spheres and soft molecules, where the latter possess an internal degree of freedom allowing bond length fluctuations. We demonstrate that the internal freedom of these soft molecules significantly influences the Soret effect. Specifically, we establish that the average internal energy of the soft molecules is non-zero and varies with the temperature gradient, thereby contributing to the heat flux. Furthermore, we derive the relationship between the Soret coefficient and the ratio of the kinetic to internal degrees of freedom, revealing that this coefficient can be either positive or negative. Throwing actions are highly adaptable, allowing individuals to adjust to various contextual factors, such as the target's location, the object's weight, and the specific task requirements. Consequently, the kinematics of these movements are influenced by multiple variables, including the point of release (PoR). While prior research has primarily focused on how the PoR affects the mechanics of the throwing limb, this study examines the impact of an incorrect PoR on the entire throwing chain. To achieve this, we utilized a multi-segment throwing model to simulate scenarios where the PoR was shifted anteriorly or posteriorly. Our findings indicate that while the throwing limb can adapt to these PoR changes, the non-throwing limb fails to compensate adequately, resulting in a significant loss of mechanical efficiency. Furthermore, the throwing limb's ability to mitigate these efficiency losses diminishes as the PoR moves further from the optimal position. These results suggest that the PoR is a critical factor in optimizing throwing efficiency. Additionally, our simulations reveal that the non-throwing limb plays a more significant role in the early phases of the movement, whereas the throwing limb becomes more dominant during the late phases. This temporal division of labor may explain why the non-throwing limb struggles to adjust to PoR variations during the late stages of the throw. Overall, this research highlights the complex interplay between the upper and lower limbs in throwing and underscores the importance of the PoR in achieving optimal performance. These insights could inform the design of assistive devices and rehabilitation protocols aimed at enhancing throwing efficiency. We introduce shallow shades, a method for estimating expectation values of Pauli observables using low-depth random Clifford circuits. This approach is designed to mitigate measurement errors caused by Pauli noise, which is prevalent in current quantum hardware. By integrating shallow shades with the shadow tomography protocol, we achieve a significant reduction in the number of quantum measurements required to determine multiple expectation values. Our findings indicate that shallow shades can be implemented on near-term devices, offering a practical pathway for extracting meaningful data from noisy quantum computations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that shallow shades can be utilized to identify and correct errors within noisy quantum circuits. This capability enables the execution of complex algorithms on near-term hardware while maintaining the accuracy of the results. We validate the efficacy of shallow shades by applying them to the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) algorithm, successfully calculating the ground state energy of the Heisenberg model on a 1D chain of 16 qubits. Additionally, we show that shallow shades can be employed to generate random quantum circuits with specific properties, such as those exhibiting high randomness. These results establish shallow shades as a valuable tool for advancing quantum computing research and development. The source code for shallow shades is publicly accessible at https://github.com/quantum-machine-learning/shallow-shades. This paper investigates the damage function, which measures the reduction in output resulting from a specific quantity of capital destruction. We demonstrate that the damage function is not merely a relationship between output and capital, but rather a complex interaction involving output, capital, and the speed at which capital recovers post-damage. Consequently, the damage function cannot be derived solely from a production function. Furthermore, we establish that the damage function exhibits an S-shaped curve, indicating that the economy is more resilient to damage when capital levels are either very low or very high. Finally, we examine the implications of these findings for the study of disasters. Our analysis reveals that the speed of capital recovery significantly influences the impact of destruction, suggesting that disasters are less damaging to economies with faster capital recovery rates. Additionally, we find that the damage function is highly sensitive to the elasticity of output with respect to capital, meaning that minor variations in this elasticity can lead to substantial differences in the estimated damage function. These insights underscore the necessity of accounting for the speed of capital recovery when analyzing the effects of destruction. Finally, we explore the implications of our findings for disaster policy. We show that policies aimed at reducing the speed of capital recovery can inadvertently increase the damage caused by destruction, thereby reducing overall welfare. This highlights the critical importance of considering the speed of capital recovery when designing disaster policies. Deep learning models are increasingly vital for data-driven decisions across diverse fields, including healthcare, finance, and marketing. However, their development is often hindered by the need for specialized expertise and the high computational costs associated with training and inference. This paper introduces MMLSpark, a unified machine learning platform designed to facilitate the creation of deep learning models for both cloud and edge environments. Built upon the open-source Apache Spark framework, MMLSpark offers a comprehensive suite of tools for data preparation, model training, and deployment. The platform's architecture is modular, enabling the integration of new algorithms and data processing techniques as research advances. Furthermore, MMLSpark supports the creation of adaptable models that can be retrained with new data to adapt to evolving data distributions. This capability is essential for maintaining model accuracy over time and for deploying deep learning systems in resource-constrained settings. The paper also explores the application of MMLSpark in edge computing, demonstrating how the platform can optimize deep learning workloads for deployment on devices with limited resources. Finally, the authors present a case study utilizing MMLSpark to develop a deep learning model for predicting stock prices, highlighting the platform's ease of use and scalability. This case study underscores MMLSpark's potential to democratize deep learning, making it more accessible to a broader range of users. Overall, this paper illustrates how MMLSpark can streamline the deep learning workflow, from data preparation to model deployment, while offering the flexibility to incorporate new algorithms and techniques as research progresses. By addressing the challenges of accessibility and scalability, MMLSpark aims to empower a wider community of practitioners and researchers to leverage the power of deep learning. The platform's modular design and support for edge computing make it a valuable tool for developing and deploying deep learning systems in real-world applications. Ultimately, MMLSpark represents a significant step towards democratizing deep learning and enabling its widespread adoption across various industries. The authors believe that MMLSpark will play a crucial role in advancing the field of deep learning and facilitating its application in diverse real-world scenarios. By providing a unified platform for data preparation, model training, and deployment, MMLSpark will help researchers and practitioners overcome the barriers to entry and accelerate the adoption of deep learning technologies. The platform's ability to adapt to changing data distributions and its support for edge computing make it an invaluable resource for developing robust and efficient deep learning systems. We introduce a new zero-shot voice translation approach that utilizes a single multilingual TTS model to execute end-to-end translation from any source language to any target language. This method requires no neural adaptation or training data for unseen language pairs and achieves state-of-the-art performance in voice translation for all known language pairs. Our system operates by first performing automatic speech recognition (ASR) on the input speech, followed by text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis of the translated output. We demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms prior methods, including those that utilize multiple models for ASR and TTS. Furthermore, we show that zero-shot translation is feasible even when the source and target languages belong to different language families. Finally, we highlight the potential of our method for cross-lingual applications, such as voice assistants, where a single TTS model can serve all supported languages. This study examines a Coleman-Gurtin type system featuring dynamic boundary constraints, where the boundary temperature and heat flux are governed by nonlinear functions of the boundary temperature. The analysis demonstrates the existence of a unique global solution to this system. Furthermore, it establishes the exponential decay of the solution within the energy space, provided the boundary functions are linear. Finally, the paper explores the long-time behavior of the solution, proving that it converges exponentially to the unique equilibrium state. These findings are supported by illustrative examples. The work extends the research conducted by the first author in reference [1]. Additionally, the methodology employed here is applicable to other systems, such as the thermoelastic system analyzed by the same author in reference [2].

This study introduces a novel probabilistic probabilistic (PP) model designed to forecast the daily peak load for low-voltage networks. The model integrates two distinct input data sources: (1) a high-resolution (15-minute) load profile generated via a long short-term memory (LSTM) network through the fusion of multiple predictive models, and (2) a daily load profile derived from the former. The proposed approach is evaluated using real-world data from a low-voltage network in the Netherlands. Results demonstrate that the model achieves a 10% reduction in the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) compared to the state-of-the-art deterministic model by Van der Vlugt et al. (2019). Furthermore, the PP model exhibits superior performance in capturing the peak load's magnitude and the variability surrounding this maximum value. These findings indicate that the proposed model is particularly well-suited for applications requiring the prediction of daily peak loads. The COVID-19 pandemic has caused significant global loss of life, with the World Health Organization reporting over 100 million confirmed cases and nearly 2 million deaths as of May 2021. While medical imaging is crucial for diagnosing and treating the disease, it remains a labor-intensive process requiring expert radiologists to manually localize and segment lesions. Accurately localizing and segmenting vertebrae in computed tomography (CT) scans is a critical step for numerous clinical tasks, including surgical planning, radiation therapy, and biomechanical analysis. This study introduces a novel framework that integrates a spine rectification network with an anatomically-constrained optimization process to achieve vertebra recognition and segmentation. The network utilizes a multi-scale architecture to extract features from various levels of the input volume, which are then fed into a multi-task loss function to simultaneously predict vertebral levels and segment individual vertebrae. To enhance the model's robustness, we developed a data augmentation strategy that incorporates random deformations. Furthermore, we implemented an anatomically-constrained optimization step that leverages the predicted vertebral levels to refine the segmentation outcomes. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach effectively and efficiently localizes and segments vertebrae across the entire spine. We investigate the scattering of a free electron by a laser field within a cavity, focusing on the ultrastrong coupling regime where the field interacts with a material. This scenario is modeled using a cavity QED framework that incorporates the electron's dynamics. We demonstrate that the electron's motion can be stabilized through its interaction with the cavity field, which is itself coupled to the material. This stabilization mechanism relies on the interference between the electron's momentum and its oscillations induced by the laser field. Furthermore, we show that this dynamical stabilization can be enhanced by exploiting vacuum oscillations between the cavity's ground and excited states. These findings are particularly relevant for systems involving the interaction of free electrons with light in the vicinity of materials, such as graphene, which exhibit strong coupling with confined electromagnetic fields. Additionally, our results may have implications for the study of relativistic electrons in strong laser fields. Finally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the electron's scattering cross-section and the cavity's emission spectrum. These results are derived using a perturbative approach that remains valid in the ultrastrong coupling regime, provided the laser field is sufficiently weak. We also outline the necessary conditions for this perturbative method to hold. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending this approach to describe the dynamics of multiple electrons. This study examines the problem of distinguishing between two non-orthogonal quantum states, $\rho$ and $\sigma$, which represent density matrices for two quantum systems. We introduce a method to calculate the optimal probability of correctly identifying these states. Our approach involves minimizing a functional that quantifies the error probability associated with distinguishing the two systems. This functional is expressed using the relative entropy between two specific sets of operators. We demonstrate that this variational problem can be transformed into an equivalent form involving the relative entropy between two sets of pure states. Furthermore, we establish that the optimal operator minimizing this functional corresponds to the solution of a linear operator equation. Finally, we apply this derived solution to the specific scenario of distinguishing two pure states. The paper concludes with a discussion of the method's potential applications. Additionally, we show that the well-known Helstrom bound emerges as a special case of our general variational framework. This work is a collaboration with Dr. A. Miranowicz. This paper addresses the challenge of solving linear operator equations $Ax=b$ within Banach spaces, where the operator $A$ is compact and linear, and the data $b$ is assumed to be noisy. We demonstrate that the dual gradient descent method, when applied to a specific Tikhonov functional, yields solutions that are both stable and optimal. Finally, we illustrate the application of this approach to problems involving the recovery of functions from their Fourier or Laplace transforms. The study includes numerical experiments that validate the theoretical findings. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of the dual gradient descent method with other established techniques for handling ill-posed problems. We employ the double field theory framework to investigate non-Riemannian gravitational actions, specifically focusing on theories characterized by torsion and the teleparallelism of the connection. By utilizing a generalized double field theory action, we derive the corresponding Riemannian geometries and identify the associated non-Riemannian fields. Furthermore, we establish a field redefinition that connects the torsional double field theory with the teleparallelism of the connection. Finally, we examine the cosmological implications of these theories, demonstrating that the teleparallelism of the connection yields a cosmological constant, whereas torsion results in a non-zero scale factor. These findings indicate that both torsion and the teleparallelism of the connection can be incorporated into the double field theory formalism. Additionally, we explore the potential of this approach for developing a non-Riemannian generalization of string theory. This research is supported by the grant number 2016/23050-0. The proliferation of wireless devices has created significant challenges for IEEE 802.11 networks, primarily due to increased channel contention and interference. To address these issues, the IEEE 802.11k/v standards were introduced to enhance network performance through channel load monitoring and link quality improvement. This paper presents a system designed to assist IEEE 802.11k/v-compliant access points (APs) and extender nodes in selecting optimal channel loads. The system utilizes a channel load estimation algorithm that accounts for both the number of active stations and their transmission rates. Additionally, it incorporates a hysteresis-based mechanism to prevent frequent channel switching. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed system effectively reduces channel load, thereby increasing the network's overall capacity. Furthermore, the system exhibits robustness against fluctuations in the number of stations and transmission rates. Finally, the system was implemented on a real-world network to validate its practicality. The proposed solution is available as open-source software at https://github.com/rajkumar1994/ChannelLoad-Aware-AP-Extender-Choice.
